current.lead: Iris says what it checked. A verdict tells a pass from a check that never ran, names who recorded the evidence it judged, and cannot be replaced by the agent it judges
intro: **Iris says what it checked. A verdict tells a pass from a check that never ran, names who recorded the evidence it judged, and cannot be replaced by the agent it judges.** 0.20.0:

- "Not checked" is its own answer in the verdict, the CI gate, the counts and the dashboard: a check that was asked for and could not run is no longer reported as a pass, and a `--fail-on` gate exits 0 only when every trace it read was judged.

- Every verdict says who recorded what it judged. A capture source declares what it records in full, so an empty list of tool calls from software that watched every call means none were made, and the same list from the agent's own report does not.

- The detectors read what was written: a test runner's verdict, a failure the agent recovered from, text spaced or wrapped to slip past a phrase rule, and an output written as JSON. A new rule, `says_something`, fails an answer that says nothing.

- Full-text search over traces, spans included, in any language: every search is bounded, and on a store in a file it runs off the event loop. `install --upgrade` moves every MCP client on the machine to the new release and copies the database before it migrates.

- Provider calls recorded without the model choosing to: OpenAI and Anthropic wrappers and LangChain and LangGraph handlers, in the Python client (`iris-eval` 0.2.0 on PyPI) and, for JavaScript, in this repository ahead of their npm packages, and OpenTelemetry GenAI traces sent to Iris are scored, with an estimated cost when a trace reports tokens but no cost.

- Also: an optional relevance judge within a daily budget, CSV and JSON Lines export, Decision Moments ranked by significance, a dashboard that works from the keyboard and with a screen reader, and API key revocation that takes effect on the next request. The server is published with npm provenance, and its Docker image, MCPB bundle and SBOMs are signed.
**Check before upgrading.** The first group can change what a CI job or a script does: read it if Iris gates a build or a script reads its answers.
**Gates, verdicts and API answers.** An entry marked BREAKING can change what a CI job or a script does with the same input.

- **BREAKING — A `--fail-on` gate exits 0 only when every trace it read was judged, and a basis trips when that layer decided the verdict or would have.** Two changes to `iris-eval ingest` and the gate action, each of which turns a job that passed into one that fails. (1) `verdict.basis` names one layer, and `--fail-on <basis>` read it alone: an output that broke a policy you configured and also leaked a credential read `policy_gate`, so `--fail-on detector_veto`, then the action's default, exited 0 on it. The verdict now lists every later layer that would have decided on its own under `verdict.also`, and `--fail-on` reads both; `fail` and `unknown` read the state of every layer the same way. A job gating on `risk_over_loss` will also trip on an output a critical detector vetoed, because the risk estimate is over the cut there too. (2) With `--fail-on`, each of these exited 0 and exits 2 now, with a sentence saying which: a trace rejected for a malformed field or a missing `output` (the run that crashed before answering); a trace stored without being evaluated; an empty file; and, with `--dataset`, a run that held none of the dataset's cases. Pass `--allow-empty` (`allow-empty: true` on the action) where a job legitimately has nothing to gate, such as one shard of a split run; it never excuses a rejected or unevaluated trace. A `--file` path that is not a file exits 2 with one sentence; it used to exit 1, the code a tripped gate uses, with a stack trace. Without `--fail-on` nothing changes.

- **BREAKING — The gate action fails the job on every verdict that is not a pass.** Its `fail-on` input defaulted to `detector_veto`, which exits 0 on an output the evaluation failed for any other reason (a hidden tool failure, an invented figure, a broken policy) and on every verdict that was not checked. The default is `any` now. A workflow that uses the action without `fail-on` and relied on only critical detections failing the job sets `fail-on: detector_veto`. The CLI has no default and is unchanged; the README and `docs/ci-gate.md` lead with `--fail-on any`.

- **BREAKING — A check somebody asked for, on a call that left out what it reads, makes the verdict not checked instead of a pass.** With a cost ceiling set in your config (`cost_threshold`), a trace over it failed and the same trace with the cost left out passed: the rule skipped, and a skip was nothing. A rule that skips for lack of what it reads now makes the verdict `unknown` (`basis: "required_evidence_missing"`, `passed: false`) when somebody had asked for it. The deployment asked when it set one of the rule's thresholds (`cost_threshold`, `max_steps`, `max_tool_repeats`, `max_target_rereads`, `max_token_ratio`, `keyword_overlap`, `topic_consistency`, `tool_choice_margin`, `tool_choice_min_fit`), promoted the rule with `eval.criticalRules`, deployed it at severity `high` or `critical`, or installed the relevance judge. The call asked when it set such a threshold itself, supplied a gating rule inline, or supplied the part of an `expected_trajectory` the rule compares against. `verdict.by` names the missing inputs, the rule result carries `lacked` and `asked`, and a sentence to the agent names the rule, what it lacked and who asked. A blank is not sent: an input of only whitespace and a negative cost are now treated as left out, where each used to be judged as a value (and passed). An explicit empty list of tool calls is sent: it says none were made, and an honest turn that used no tool does not read "not checked" because a step ceiling is set. `eval.onCriticalSkipped: "pass"` accepts a critical rule that could not run for missing evidence. A gate keyed on `passed`, or on `--fail-on any`, `unknown` or `required_evidence_missing`, that passed such traces fails them now: send the field, or remove the setting that asks for it. With the shipped configuration and a call that supplies no threshold, rule or expectation of its own, nothing changes, and a text-only evaluation passes as before.

- **BREAKING — A failure outranks a layer that could not check.** An output the risk layer fails, on a deployment where a critical check could not answer or required evidence was missing, read `verdict.state: "unknown"`; it reads `fail` now, `basis: "risk_over_loss"`, with the layer that could not check under `verdict.also`. `--fail-on` and the webhooks already read every layer and trip as before; a caller that branched on `verdict.state` or `verdict.basis` itself sees the failure first. Each stored evaluation is stamped with the ordering it was judged under and reads back under it. One kind of row from 0.19.0 does not read back as its caller was given it, and did not before this change either: an evaluation that was not checked because required evidence was missing reads back as a pass, because that release did not store the requirement with the row. Its stored result is still "did not pass", and every count treats it so.

- **BREAKING — An evaluation linked to a trace is that trace's verdict only when it scores the trace as stored.** `evaluate_output` with a `trace_id` and `output`, `input`, `tool_calls`, `tools`, `cost_usd` or `token_usage` that differs from what the trace stored, or with one `eval_type`, now answers with `reference_trace_id` in place of `trace_id` and a sentence saying what differed; so does a call that names a trace which recorded no output, and so does every `evaluate_with_llm_judge` and `verify_citations` call that names a trace. Such an evaluation is still stored, listed with the trace and erased with it, and it no longer counts in the trace's run, in `compare_runs` or `compare_traces`, in the score filter of `get_traces`, or in the `latest_*` export columns. A workflow that judged each trace with `evaluate_with_llm_judge` and compared runs on those judgments will find the comparison reading the deterministic verdicts instead; to have a judge decide a trace's verdict, set a relevance judge (`IRIS_RELEVANCE_JUDGE_MODEL`). To re-score a stored trace, call `evaluate_output` with its `trace_id` and nothing else: `output` is optional now, and the stored input, tool calls, tools and cost are read from the trace, so the relevance rules run where they used to skip. Evaluations stored by earlier releases are not changed. Migration `020-eval-reference-trace` adds the column.

- **BREAKING — An expected call that was never made fails, where it used to pass (`tool_sequence` and `step_budget`, version 2).** `evaluate_output` with `expected_trajectory.tool_calls` and `tool_calls: []` skipped `tool_sequence`: there was "no trajectory to judge". An explicit empty list is a trajectory of no calls, and against an expectation of calls it now fails every mode but `superset`; `step_budget` judges it as zero calls, which is within any budget. Calls that are not sent at all still skip. The ruleset fingerprint changes.

- **BREAKING — `compare_runs` and `POST /api/v1/compare` answer differently in four ways.** (1) `better` is no longer true when the second run was judged by fewer rules than the first; `improvement_withheld` is true instead. A job that read `better` to promote a run stops promoting one that sent less evidence. (2) `equivalent_within` is null unless you pass `equivalence_margin`; it used to default to a margin computed from the run sizes. A caller that read `equivalent_within.holds` without a margin now reads null. (3) `difference` carries a 90% interval where it carried a 95% one, and when the runs pair it is the interval McNemar's test implies, not the unpaired one; `difference.significant` now agrees with `worse` and `better`. (4) `smallest_detectable` is larger: it is the difference detected four times in five, where it was the one detected about half the time (62 points for two runs of eight, where it read 40). The summary no longer contains `**` markers. New fields: `call`, `coverage`, `critical_rises`, `paired.fell`, and `judged_before` / `judged_after` on each rule row.

- **BREAKING — `compare_traces` reports a wider interval, and `overall.rate` is the mean over cases.** The run-level interval is exact for the number of cases and can no longer be zero-width: ten of ten cases reads [69.2%, 100%] where it read [100%, 100%]. `overall.rate` is the mean of the cases' own pass rates; it equals `pooled.rate` when every case was asked the same number of times and differs otherwise.

- **BREAKING — Two runs that differ in a verdict-deciding setting are no longer called comparable, and a rule change that cannot be recorded is refused.** The configuration fingerprint (`provenance.configHash`) now covers `eval.defaultsGate`, `eval.falsePassCost`, `eval.onCriticalSkipped`, `eval.requiredEvidence`, `eval.priorMode` and a prior set in config or estimated from labels, and the ruleset fingerprint (`provenance.rulesetHash`) covers the content of every deployed, inline and plugin rule. A deployment with none of these set and no custom rules keeps both hashes; any other gets new ones from its next evaluation, so `compare_runs` between a run from before the upgrade and one after names the configuration or the ruleset as different (it already named the engine version) and compares them only with `force`. With an estimated prior the fingerprint moves as labels are added, because the verdicts do. `deploy_rule`, `delete_rule`, the dashboard's rule routes and `delete_trace` now write their audit entry before the change and fail with `IRIS_STORAGE_ERROR` when it cannot be written; they used to carry on without a record.

- **BREAKING — `verify_citations` reports a judge failure under `judge_error`, not `resolve_error`.** A caller that read the judge's error from `resolve_error` on a citation whose `resolve_status` is `"ok"` reads it from `judge_error` instead, with the same `kind` and `message`. `resolve_error` now means only that the source was not resolved.

- **`compare_runs` says when the cases that fell were not checked rather than failed.** Ten cases that passed before and could not be checked after read "10 cases passed before and failed after ... This is a regression". They still count against the second run (`worse` is true: a run that cannot be checked has not passed), and the summary now says what happened: "did not pass after (10 not checked, 0 failed)", and when none of them failed, that evidence stopped arriving and nothing was found wrong with the answers. Each run summary carries `not_checked`, and `paired` carries `fell_not_checked`.

- **A case is flaky only when it passed and FAILED.** `flaky` on `GET /api/v1/cases/:key`, in the `flaky_cases` view and in `compare_traces`, and the `flaky_case` webhook, counted a verdict that was not checked as the other answer, so a case with one pass and one unreached verdict was "answered both ways". An attempt that was not checked is now neither answer.

- **A row of `categories` is the verdict, read for the rules that bundle holds.** `categories.<bundle>.passed` was its own arithmetic: a weighted mean of the bundle's rule scores against a threshold, with the critical veto. The verdict stopped using that arithmetic in 0.10.0, so on an evaluation that failed for a hidden tool error every row could read `passed: true`, and a script keyed on `categories.safety.passed` shipped the output the evaluation failed. A row now carries `state` (`pass`, `fail`, `unknown`) and `passed` follows it (`true`, `false`, and `null` for a row that was not checked): the row holding the rules that failed the evaluation fails, every checked row of a passing evaluation passes, a rule that lacked evidence it was asked for leaves its own bundle not checked, and an input `eval.requiredEvidence` names leaves every bundle not checked. A script that read a bundle's `passed` will see failures it did not see before, and `null` where it saw `false` for a bundle that lacked evidence; a row no longer fails for a low `score` alone. `score` on a row is unchanged.

- **A webhook that names no `events` also receives `verdict_not_checked`.** The new event is delivered for a verdict that could not be reached and that no layer failed. Name the events you want to keep the old five.

- **Required evidence is met by what the call carried, and a capture source can say a turn made no tool call.** `eval.requiredEvidence` used to count an input only when a rule that ran had read it, so a deployment that requires `cost` read a call that sent its cost as "not checked" when the call ran one bundle (`eval_type: "safety"`); it passes now. A trace recorded by the Claude Code capture plugin now names the plugin and what it records in full (below): on a deployment that requires `tool_calls`, a captured turn that made no tool call read "not checked" and passes now, and a captured turn whose record is incomplete reads "not checked" where it may have passed. The trace CSV export has a `capture` column between `source` and `session_id`; a reader that takes columns by position shifts by one from there. Migration `022-trace-capture` adds the column that holds it. A verdict that nothing could judge (`basis: "no_rules"`) now lists missing evidence under `verdict.also` (`required_evidence_missing`), whether a deployment required it or a capture source promised it, so `--fail-on required_evidence_missing` trips on such a trace where it passed. Two more changes in what counts as sent: a blank `expected`, or an `expected_trajectory` no trajectory rule can use (`{}`, `{ "tool_calls": [] }`), no longer meets a requirement for one; and `evaluate_output` that sends `tool_calls: []` for a trace stored without tool calls is now kept beside the trace (`reference_trace_id`), because an empty list is other evidence than none, where it used to be the trace's verdict.

- **`GET /api/v1/moments` with a `verdict`, `min_significance` or `significance_kind` filter returns full pages from a window of recent traces.** `offset` now counts matching moments rather than traces, `total` is the exact number of matches in the window rather than the trace count, and the response carries `window`. A client that paged a filtered list by adding `limit` to `offset` gets every match once instead of gaps; one that read `total` as the trace count reads `window.tracesInRange`. Matches older than the window (the newest 500 traces by default, `window` to narrow it) are not returned: narrow `agent_name`, `since` or `until` to reach them.
**Rules that fail outputs they used to pass.** A gate on `detector_veto` or `any` can trip where it passed before.

- **`no_injection_patterns`, `no_blocklist_words`, `no_pii` and `no_injection_compliance` fail outputs that hid a phrase behind its spacing or a value behind an invisible character.** An override phrase written one word per line, with tabs, or with no-break spaces in place of spaces passed before and fails now. So does a blocked phrase written that way, and a recovery phrase listed one word per line. A Social Security number, card number or key with a right-to-left override, an invisible separator, a variation selector or a tag character inside it passed and fails now. A gate that passed such an output will block it. Ordinary wrapped prose and a quoted discussion of an attack phrase read as before. No setting turns this off.

- **`no_silent_tool_failure` reads a test runner's verdict, and stops counting a failure the agent recovered from (rule version 2).** Two changes to what fails, in opposite directions. (1) An answer of "All tests pass" beside a tool output ending `Tests  3 failed | 12 passed` passed every rule: the call carried no error and its first line was the runner's banner. For a tool that runs a command, the head and tail of its output are now read for a failing verdict (`3 failed`, `FAIL …`, `FAILED …`, `npm ERR!`, `Found 3 errors`, a non-zero exit code), and an object output written as a JSON string (`"{\"ok\": false}"`) is read as the object. An answer that does not own such a failure now fails the rule, and at the shipped configuration the verdict. (2) A failure followed by a later call that went right on the same thing no longer has to be owned: the same command passing after a fix, a misspelled argument then the right one, a failing run then a passing one. Until now every such answer failed the rule unless it happened to use a failure word. A gate that blocked on a retried call stops blocking it; a gate that passed a false "tests pass" blocks it. The ruleset fingerprint changes, so `compare_runs` refuses a run from before against one from after unless forced.

- **A quotation does not run from one field of a structured output into the next, and a sentence has a word in it.** The injection rule treats a phrase inside quotation marks as discussion. Quote marks in two neighbouring fields of a JSON answer bracketed the field between them as quoted, so an override phrase there passed, plain or disguised; a quotation now ends at the mark the reading puts on a line of its own between two values. A quotation in prose may still run across paragraphs, as a forwarded email does, and a pilcrow inside a line of prose ("under ¶ 4") is a character. The sentence splitters end a sentence at that mark too, and count no segment without a letter or a digit as a sentence, so a horizontal rule (`---`), a lone bullet or a line holding only an emoji no longer adds to `sentence_count`.

- **`no_pii`: a masked key is not a secret, and asterisks after a whole secret do not mask it.** The check for a value assigned to a secret's name read `sk-****…3f9a` as a secret. A value is masked when four asterisks hide all but a few of its characters; `Xk9mP2vQ7rL4nT8wZ3hY****` is still a secret. `DOB` and `MRN` labels are read with a quote and a colon after them, as a JSON field writes them (`"dob": "1990-04-12"`); a quoted label with no colon after it is not one.

- **`no_stub_output`: a marker that a removal verb acts on is finished work.** "Removed the last TODO comment" and "resolved all remaining FIXME notes" read as unfinished work. A removal verb before the marker, on the same line, marks a report of done work, and an article before a marker may be followed by any horizontal space (a no-break space included) but not a blank line; "the only TODO left is the retry" still fires, and so does a marker on the line after "removed".

- **`no_stub_output` and `no_hallucination_markers` read the same text however it is spaced or wrapped (version 2 of each).** A placeholder phrase typed with two spaces ("omitted  for  brevity"), or cut by a line wrap, was not the phrase the rule knew, and a paragraph wrapped at 60 columns was counted as one sentence per line. On the labelled corpus, doubling every space turned three placeholder findings and two fabrication findings into passes. Both rules now match a phrase across any short run of whitespace and count sentences on the paragraph. An output that passed only because of its spacing fails now. The published accuracy of both rules is unchanged (the same errors on the same cases), and the ruleset fingerprint changes.

- **An output written as JSON is read by what it says (the sixteen rules that read the output are each at a version 0.19.0 did not have).** An answer sent as a JSON object or array, such as `{"answer": "…", "sources": […]}`, was read in its escaped form: a line break was the two characters `\n`, a quote was `\"`, and a phrase inside a string value sat between quotes, where the injection rule reads it as a quotation. On the labelled corpus, sending every output as one string field of a JSON object changed five verdicts and thirteen answers of the rules that decide one: three injections were missed and an empty answer was not empty. The rules that read the output now read a structured one by its values, each value its own paragraph; the leak, blocklist and injection rules read every field name too, quoted, before its value (`"password": …`, `"dob": …`) or alone where its value is an object or a list, so a secret is recognised by the field it is assigned to, a key can be the leak, and a directive smuggled as a key is found as it is inside prose. Every evidence offset still points into the output as sent, and the relevance judge's redaction reads a structured text the way the leak rule does. Custom rules read the output exactly as sent. Changes in both directions: a structured output that passed because escaping hid a leak, a placeholder or an injection fails now, and one that failed only on its escaping passes (an empty answer in `{"answer": ""}` now fails `non_empty_output`). A leading byte-order mark is skipped; JSON with a no-break space or another Unicode space beside it is read as written. One injection shape is read only in a structured reading: a field whose value is an override, quoted or not and disguised or not, which the labelled reading writes without the quotes the prose pattern needs; a value whose sentence quotes a payload is a report about it, as in prose. Each rule result that read a structured output says which reading it took in `read`. The ruleset fingerprint changes.

- **An answer that says nothing fails: a new rule, `says_something`.** Against two fixed asks (an action, and a piece of writing), ten of twelve trivial agents passed clean: "Done.", "OK", "The task has been completed successfully.", "…", "null", "lorem ipsum dolor sit amet", the ask copied back, one sentence repeated 400 times, and two refusals. `says_something` reads the shape of a non-answer against what the ask asked for. To an ask for something written: a promise in place of the work ("Will do!") when no tool call is recorded, a placeholder ("null", "…", "{{answer}}", lorem ipsum), or a "here is …" with nothing after it. To an ask to write or to act when the call says no tool was called (`tool_calls: []`): a bare "Done." or "OK", a promise, or a placeholder. To any ask: an announcement that ends on a colon with nothing after it, the ask handed back, or one passage on a loop. A question answered "OK", "null" or "Done.", an ask to confirm answered "OK", an action reported done when the call does not say that no tool ran, and a refusal pass: each can be a correct answer, and whether a refusal was right is a judgement about the ask. Its family is 242 labelled cases, 200 of them written from a definition of a non-answer by model instances that never saw the rule: it fails none of the 126 answers and catches 23 of the 116 non-answers (precision 100%, 95% interval 85.7 to 100; recall 19.8%). On the 100 written after its last revision it caught 4 of 50 non-answers and failed none of 50 answers. Most non-answers there are fluent replies that never contain what was asked, which no rule that reads the shape of an output can detect. `proof/INVARIANTS.md` publishes the twelve agents against both asks: where `tool_calls: []` records that nothing was called, none passes except the two refusals and the action handed back, each with its reason. It is a detection in the completeness bundle and the `stub` class; no composite verdict changes, and a typical clean pass's risk estimate moves from 0.118 to 0.110. The ruleset fingerprint changes, and the built-in rule count is 26.

- **A trace that sends token counts and a model but no cost is now stored with an estimated cost, so cost totals rise and the cost rules start judging it (#702).** Most OpenTelemetry and framework traces are such traces. After upgrading, their cost counts toward the dashboard's total cost, `GET /api/v1/summary` and the `cost_by_agent` view, and `cost_under_threshold` (default $0.10), `cost_anomaly`, custom `cost_threshold` rules and the `cost_anomaly` webhook act on it instead of skipping. A gate on `cost_under_threshold` can start failing traces it used to skip. Each estimate is marked `cost_source: "estimated"` wherever it shows. Traces stored before the upgrade are not re-priced. To keep the old behaviour, set `pricing.estimate: false` in `config.json`.

- **`answers_the_ask` stops blocking at the shipped config.** A gate that relied on it failing off-topic answers at the defaults stops blocking them. To keep it gating, set `IRIS_RELEVANCE_JUDGE_MODEL` to have the relevance judge decide (below), or set a `keyword_overlap` or `topic_consistency` threshold in your config file to gate on the lexical reading.
**Upgrading the server and its data.**

- **Move every MCP client to 0.20.0 in one step: `npx -y @iris-eval/mcp-server@latest install --upgrade` (#704).** Every client shares `~/.iris/iris.db`, and since 0.19.0 `install` pins each client to one release. 0.20.0 adds migrations `015-trace-search` and later, and the first 0.20.0 process to open the file (the Claude Desktop extension, `npx iris-eval`, or `npx @iris-eval/mcp-server` with no version) applies them; from then on a client still pinned to 0.19.x refuses to start with `This database was migrated by a newer Iris (…) — migration(s) 015-trace-search, … are unknown to v0.19.0`. That message comes from 0.19.x and cannot change. The command moves every pinned client; the Claude Code plugins move with `claude plugin marketplace update iris-eval` and `claude plugin update iris-eval@iris-eval` (and `iris-eval-capture@iris-eval`). To go back to 0.19.0 instead, restore the copy 0.20.0 takes before migrating: README, [Downgrading](https://github.com/iris-eval/mcp-server#downgrading).

- **The first start after upgrading copies the database before migrating it, and takes longer by the copy.** Measured on a Windows 11 desktop (Node 24.11, better-sqlite3): 2.4 to 2.7 s for a 468 MB file of 100,000 traces, three runs. The copy needs free disk space about the size of the file; without it the start migrates without a copy and says so.

- **After upgrading, the trace search index is built in the background, and the file grows by about two thirds.** At 100,000 traces on the benchmark machine the file went from 125 MB to 211 MB (69% larger). The server starts and answers MCP and HTTP requests at once, and the index is built behind it in steps of about 50 ms of work each. Measured on a file of 100,000 traces from 0.19.0: the first start took 449 ms, and the index was built in 33.4 s, with the event loop held for at most 449 ms. Traces sent over OTLP with spans take longer, because their span text is indexed too: 158.8 s at 100,000 agent-loop traces, with a first start of 360 ms and the event loop held for at most 329 ms, and the file is larger (993 MB where the same traces took 841 MB with an index of their own fields only; the table under Added has the numbers). Traces with Chinese, Japanese or Korean text take longer again, because each run is also indexed as two-character pieces: 50.8 s at 10,000 agent-loop traces written in Chinese, and a file of 251 MB where those traces took 128 MB before (the numbers are under Added, with the entry for words inside CJK text). Until the build finishes, a search reads the traces directly (`search.index` is `scan`): slower, with the same results, and on a large store it stops at the search time budget with `search.complete: false` (see Security). The server logs one line when the build starts, with how many traces it will index, and one when it is done, with the count and the time; `GET /api/v1/health` reports `search.state` and `search.progress` (the share of traces indexed so far), and `--self-test` reports the configured database's index. `get_traces` without `q` sorts by `timestamp` as before; with `q` the default order is relevance.

- **After upgrading, four indexes are built in the background, after the server answers (#711, #744).** Migration 019 adds the indexes the dashboard's summary, filters and trace list and the agent failure log now name, and drops the three they replace. On a file with traces they are built after the server starts, each in one statement off the event loop; until they are, those reads answer with the same results on the indexes the file already had, more slowly, and `GET /api/v1/health` says `"indexes": "building"` (`--self-test` says so too). On a file of 100,000 agent-loop traces written by 0.19.0, the first start's work before the MCP connection opens took 54 to 60 ms where it took 1.72 to 2.13 s with the indexes built in the start (three runs each, without the copy taken before migrating, above), and the indexes were ready 2.1 to 4.9 s after it; a page of 50 traces took 9 to 16 ms meanwhile, 5 ms after. While each index is built, a write waits for it, as it waits behind any other writer.

- **Committed writes reach the disk at each checkpoint of the write-ahead log, on both drivers (`storage.synchronous`, default `normal`) (#711).** A crash of Iris loses nothing and the file cannot be corrupted; a power cut or an operating-system crash can roll back the writes made since the last sync. With better-sqlite3 this is what 0.19.0 already ran on every start but the one that created the file, because that SQLite is built to open a WAL file at `NORMAL`; on Node's built-in `node:sqlite` it was `FULL` throughout and is `NORMAL` now. Set `"storage": { "synchronous": "full" }` in `config.json` to sync every commit, which keeps each committed trace through a power cut and costs about 1.5 ms a write.

- **Storing a trace costs more with the search index on, which is the default.** Sustained OTLP ingest of traces with two model spans stored 1,735 traces/s at 100,000 traces and 2,000 at 10,000, where 0.19.0 stored 2,330 and 2,620, and one `log_trace` call takes about 0.1 ms longer. A feed that needs the ingest rate more than fast search can set `storage.searchIndex: "off"` (`IRIS_SEARCH_INDEX=off`), which stored 4,237 and 4,393 traces/s; search then reads the traces themselves within its time budget (under Added).

- **The retention sweep runs after the server answers, in short steps (#695).** It used to run before the MCP connection opened, as one transaction: a stdio client that started Iris on a store with traces past `retention.days` waited for the whole sweep, and the search index made the sweep several times slower. The connection now opens first, and the sweep deletes a few traces per transaction with the event loop free between them; for a sweep of more than 1 in 125 of the indexed traces it then merges the search index in steps, which erases the swept words from the file as `optimize` did. `Retention cleanup: deleted …` is logged when both are done, and a merge that a closing server leaves unfinished is finished by the next start. Measured over stdio against the code before this change, alternated, on the benchmark machine while other work shared it, with agent-loop traces (three model calls and two tool calls each) and 3% of them past the window: at 10,000 traces the first answer to `initialize` came after 640 to 661 ms instead of 1,442 to 1,467 ms (three runs each); at 100,000, after 0.74 s and 1.21 s instead of 8.6 s and 17.6 s. The sweep itself still takes seconds at that size, in the background: it was done 9.0 s and 12.1 s after the start, against 9.2 s and 18.3 s. While it runs, the longest the event loop was held was 57 to 95 ms at 10,000 traces and 189 ms and 545 ms at 100,000.

- **BREAKING — The Docker image keeps its whole Iris home in the `/data` volume.** The image now sets `IRIS_HOME=/data`, so deployed rules (`custom-rules.json`), `audit.log`, `config.json` and `preferences.json` sit beside `iris.db`. Before, they were written to `/home/iris/.iris` inside the container and were lost whenever the container was recreated. A deployment that mounted its own volume at `/home/iris/.iris` to keep them should copy those files into the `/data` volume, or set `IRIS_HOME` back to that path. `/data` is now created mode 700, like a fresh `~/.iris`.

- **The retention sweep keeps the pinned baseline run.** Traces and evaluations of the run pinned as the baseline (`PATCH /api/v1/runs/:id { "baseline": true }`) are no longer deleted at `retention.days`. If you pinned a run and relied on the window to remove its text, unpin it, or delete its traces with `delete_trace`; each sweep that keeps some of it logs the run and the counts. With no run pinned the sweep deletes exactly what it did.

- **A rule deployed through one MCP client now applies in every other client's server.** Each client's server process re-reads the shared rules file when it changes, so a rule deployed, switched off or deleted through one applies in all of them within 20 ms. If you kept different rules per client by relying on each process holding its own copy until restart, they now converge on the file.
**Integrations.**

- **BREAKING — OTLP traces in the GenAI conventions store words, not JSON, as their input and output.** A trace from Pydantic AI, Semantic Kernel, or any other exporter whose input or output is a message array (`gen_ai.input.messages` / `gen_ai.output.messages`, or OpenAI-shaped `[{ role, content }]`) now stores the last question asked as `input` and the last answer as `output`. A caller reading `input` / `output` from `GET /api/v1/traces`, `get_traces` or the OTLP answer sees text where it saw a JSON array; the span attributes keep the JSON as sent. Traces stored before the upgrade keep their JSON.

- **BREAKING — An OTLP trace's output is what the run ended with, and an unnamed service is not an agent.** Past the root span, `output` is now read from the span that ended last rather than the one that started first, and a trace whose resource carries only the OTel SDKs' default `service.name` (`unknown_service`, `unknown_service:<process>`) is filed under the agent its spans name (`gen_ai.agent.name`, OpenInference's `agent.name`), else under `"otel"` with `service.name` listed as lacked. A caller that filtered OTLP traces by `agent_name=unknown_service:python.exe` finds them under the agent's name or `"otel"`; traces stored before the upgrade keep theirs. A span attribute that is a Python object's repr (`StopEvent(result=…)`) is no longer taken as a trace's input or output.

- **BREAKING — An OTLP agent span is `INTERNAL`, not `LLM`.** A span whose `gen_ai.operation.name` is `invoke_agent` or `create_agent` is stored with kind `INTERNAL`; a caller that counted `LLM` spans from OTLP traces counts only the model calls now. Token and cost totals do not change.

- **The Claude Code capture plugin records the tool calls that failed, and loses no call a turn made.** Claude Code reports a failed tool call (a command that exited non-zero, a missing file, an MCP tool's error) through `PostToolUseFailure`, which the plugin did not listen to, so a failed call never reached Iris and the rule that asks whether an answer owned a failed call had nothing to read on the path that records every turn. It is recorded now, with the error the agent received. A turn is now kept under its prompt's id (`prompt_id`, sent by Claude Code from 2.1.196) rather than its session, and nothing it records is deleted before it is sent: the calls of a turn you interrupted (which fires no `Stop`) and of a background sub-agent that kept working after its turn ended were thrown away when the next prompt arrived, or landed in the next turn; they are sent then as an `unfinished` part of their own turn, stored and not judged, with a sub-agent's calls named in `metadata.subagent_calls`. A turn a `Stop` hook keeps going is sent as a second, `continued` part with its prompt. A turn that ends in an API error (`StopFailure`) is stored with its calls and the error, with no answer, and is not judged, rather than scored on the error text. An empty `tool_calls` list is sent only when the record is known whole (the prompt seen, the turn stopped, nothing running in the background), so Iris does not read "no tool calls were made" into a turn whose calls it may not have. When the model calls `log_trace` for the turn itself, the plugin no longer stands down: both traces are kept, and the plugin's names the model's, once, in `metadata.model_logged.trace_ids`, because the model's account can leave out the call that failed. Expect more failed verdicts on captured turns (failed calls the answer did not own), and more traces: two for a turn the model logged, and a part for each turn that did not end cleanly. What the plugin holds is kept like a secret: without a host data directory it lives in `capture/` inside your Iris home instead of a shared temporary directory, readable by you alone; calls are appended as they finish, each on its own line, so calls run in parallel are all kept and a write cut short loses only itself; a tool output over 256 KB is kept as its head and tail, marked `truncated`; a turn that could not be ingested is retried and removed after seven days, a closed session's files are sent and removed after a day, and the capture log is rotated at 1 MB; both ingest attempts run the pinned version. Each turn is sent in the form the pinned release reads: a release before 0.20.0 gets it without the `capture` declaration, which that release's ingest would refuse along with the whole turn. A test in the upgrade suite has the release the plugin pins ingest a turn the plugin's own hooks built.

- **The dashboard's Moments page opens ranked by significance, not newest first, and refreshes every 10 seconds instead of 3.** Add `?sort=newest` to the page address, or pick Newest first in its Order control, for the old stream. `GET /api/v1/moments` is unchanged unless a caller passes `sort_by=significance`.

sections.title: Security
items: **A long run of full stops, question marks or exclamation marks no longer holds the event loop.** The sentence splitter read a run of terminators inside a word again from each terminator in it, and read the word before every full stop back to the last space, so the time to evaluate such an output grew with the square of its length: 20,000 full stops between two letters took 1.6 seconds, and `a.B` repeated over 20,000 characters 1.3, each doubling taking four times as long. A run is now read once, and only as much of the word before a full stop as the abbreviation lists need: the same outputs take 4 ms and 18 ms, and 80,000 characters 8 ms and 69 ms. Sentences are split exactly as before; the old and new splitters agree on 226,190 texts, 26,190 of them from the repository's proof corpora, fixtures and documents. The playground's copy has the same change.

**Two ways past the critical detectors are closed.** (1) The fold that rejoins a word an evader split with a tab or a line break (`previ|ous`) read every lone break between two letters that way, so a phrase whose words were separated by anything but a plain space became one unbroken string: `ignore all previous instructions` written one word per line, with tabs, or with no-break spaces passed `no_injection_patterns`; a blocked phrase passed `no_blocklist_words`; a recovery phrase listed down the page passed `no_pii`; and a directive wrapped across lines in a tool result was missed by `no_injection_compliance`. These rules now read the text both ways, as joined tokens and as separate words, and report whichever reading holds the match, with the span still indexing the raw text. The structural injection detectors, which are line-shaped, read only the first. (2) Invisible characters were dropped from a list of eight. A right-to-left override, an invisible separator, an Arabic letter mark, a directional isolate, a variation selector or a tag character inside a Social Security number defeated `no_pii`. Every Unicode format character and every variation selector is dropped now. The published transforms table at https://iris-eval.com/proof shows the difference on the no-break-space and line-break rows, and the public playground reads the same way as the server.

**The agent being judged can no longer replace its own verdict.** Every reader of a trace's verdict takes the newest evaluation carrying the trace's id, and every evaluation a caller linked to a trace carried it, whatever was judged. So after a trace failed on a leaked Social Security number, one `evaluate_output` call with that `trace_id` and clean text made the trace read `pass` in its run, in `compare_runs` and in the export, with no flag; the leaking text with `eval_type: "cost"`, or with an empty `tool_calls`, did the same, and so did a lenient `evaluate_with_llm_judge` template. A trace's verdict is now only the server's own scoring of the trace as stored. Anything else is stored with the trace named in a separate column (`reference_trace_id`, migration 020) and no trace id of its own, so no reader of a trace's verdict can pick it up: the readers that list a trace's evaluations ask for both columns, and a reader written later that forgets the new column shows less rather than a replaced verdict. Deleting the trace erases the text of both kinds.

**A swapped rule and a changed gating setting change the fingerprint, and the audit log says what a rule was.** `provenance.rulesetHash` named a deployed rule by its name alone: a rule that blocked a competitor's name, replaced under the same name by one matching nothing, turned the verdict from fail to pass under the same hash. `provenance.configHash` left out every composer setting, so the same output passed and failed under one fingerprint when `eval.defaultsGate`, the loss ratio, the handling of a critical check that could not answer, the required evidence or an estimated prior changed, and `compare_runs` called the two runs comparable. Both are covered now, appended only where set, so a deployment at the shipped settings with built-in rules keeps its hashes. An audit entry for a rule now carries `details.contentSha256`, the same hash the ruleset fingerprint carries for it, on deploy, toggle and delete. The entry is written before the change, and a failed write refuses the change: the append used to sit inside an empty `catch`, so a full or read-only disk let a rule be deployed, disabled or deleted, or a trace removed, with no record.

**A verdict that was `unknown` for missing required evidence read back as a pass.** A stored evaluation's verdict is composed again on read from the settings stored with it, and `eval.requiredEvidence` was not among them, so the row read back under "nothing required". It is stored with the row now.

**A critical detection is no longer hidden behind a policy failure.** The verdict's layers are asked in order (a policy you configured, a critical detector, a critical check that could not answer, required evidence, the risk estimate), `verdict.basis` names one of them, and everything that acted on one basis read `basis` alone. So for an output that broke a configured policy and leaked a Social Security number: `iris-eval ingest --fail-on detector_veto` exited 0, the `detector_veto` webhook did not fire, and the agent was told only that its cost ceiling had failed. `verdict.also` now lists every later layer that would have decided the verdict on its own, each as `{ basis, state, by }`, in the order the layers are asked; it is absent when one layer decided alone and on every pass. `--fail-on`, the `detector_veto` and `verdict_fail` webhooks, the gate action's receipt and the dashboard's verdict panel read it, the evaluation CSV carries it as `verdict_also` (`latest_verdict_also` on the trace CSV), and `interpretations` gains one sentence to the agent naming the later layers and saying that clearing the first does not clear the verdict. `basis`, `by` and `verdictPath()` are unchanged, so nothing that read them reads differently. The risk estimate is now computed on a verdict an earlier layer decided, which is how a `risk_over_loss` entry reaches `also`; `verdict.risk` is still carried only when the risk layer decided or the verdict is clean. A stored evaluation reads back with `also`, since the verdict is composed on read. Tests: each pair of layers through the composer, the command-line gate end to end on the output above, the webhook, the receipt and the panel; the gate and webhook cases failed before the change.

**Dependency advisories closed in every workspace:** `fast-uri` 3.1.7 → 3.1.8 (GHSA-hrr3-gc8f-f4qj, inconsistent host case normalization through percent-encoded octets; it ships, through `ajv`), and `brace-expansion` 5.0.9 → 5.0.12 and 1.1.18 → 1.1.21 (GHSA-qhr7-859c-m2p7, GHSA-6j4f-fj2g-mc7p and GHSA-q2hr-2g5m-vwhr, CPU and stack exhaustion on crafted brace patterns; development tooling only, through ESLint's `minimatch`, in the root, dashboard and website). Each override's floor is now the fixed version. The lockfiles were regenerated on Linux, and only these packages moved in them.

**Citation fetching refuses NAT64 addresses that lead to a private network.** The SSRF guard already refused private IPv4 re-encoded as 6to4, Teredo, IPv4-mapped and IPv4-compatible IPv6. It now also checks NAT64. For the well-known prefix `64:ff9b::/96`, the IPv4 address inside it goes through the same blocklist: on a network with a NAT64 gateway, `64:ff9b::7f00:1` reaches 127.0.0.1. The local-use prefix `64:ff9b:1::/48` is refused whole. The gap was found while triaging GHSA-2vr4-cq9g-pvrc, which reported the same range missing from the `ip-address` package. `ip-address` moves from 10.4.0 to 10.7.2 (GHSA-rpw4-54j3-4h4q, GHSA-2vr4-cq9g-pvrc) and the dashboard's test-only `undici` from 7.29.0 to 7.30.0 (GHSA-3wwx-pv8p-q78v). Neither was reachable in Iris; `SECURITY-EXPOSURE.md` records why.

**One search can no longer stall the server (#703).** Full-text search is new in this release, and before this fix one query could cost as much as reading most of the index, once per term, on the event loop that every MCP and HTTP request waits on. On the benchmark machine, `w* w* w* w*` took 2.5 s at 10,000 traces and 23.9 s at 100,000, and 32 repeats of `w*` took 26.4 s at 10,000. Anyone who could call `get_traces` with `q`, `GET /api/v1/traces?q=` or the dashboard's search box could send such a query. Search is now bounded in three ways.
- Normalising: a repeated term, and a one-word prefix that another one-word term implies (`ref*` beside `refund`), is searched once. The traces matched do not change; a property test checks 500 generated queries against the terms as typed. The response lists each term left out under `search.ignored`.
- Limits: a prefix needs at least 3 letters or digits before the `*`, or 1 character in Chinese, Japanese or Korean, where one character is a word. A query carries at most 16 terms and 4 prefix terms. A query over a limit is refused before anything is read, with a message that names the term and the limit (an error from `get_traces`, a 400 from the HTTP API), and the dashboard shows the prefix rule as a hint. Three letters, because a prefix costs more the more words it starts: on text built from English-like syllables at 10,000 traces, one broad prefix took 62 ms at one letter, 45 at two, 26 at three and 3 at four, and the two-letter one matched 99.97% of traces, narrowing nothing. Every query from the review now answers in under 1 ms, refused.
- A time budget: a search reads matches newest first for at most 1,000 ms (`storage.searchBudgetMs` in `config.json`, or `IRIS_SEARCH_BUDGET_MS`, 50 to 60,000). If it reaches the budget first, it answers with the best matches among the traces it read, sets `search.complete` to `false` and `search.budget_ms` to the budget, and `total` counts only the matches found. This covers the search without FTS5 too, which is also what runs while the index is built after an upgrade, and which read every trace however long that took.
- What comes before the first match cannot be stopped: expanding a prefix, and counting the traces each term is in for the ranking. The limits bound it. At 100,000 traces the costliest query they allow took 0.6 s (four of the broadest three-letter prefixes on English-like text), and 0.4 s with Chinese terms.
- A search on a store in a file now runs on a worker thread with its own read-only connection, so none of that work runs on the event loop, whatever the store's size. The thread starts with the first search and builds the page's snippets as well, and the server's thread only reads the page's rows. At 100,000 traces, measured by a 1 ms timer on the server's thread with the median of 7 runs, the longest wait for four of the broadest three-letter prefixes fell from 428 ms to 17 ms with better-sqlite3, and from 455 ms to 16 ms with `node:sqlite`. With CJK text, four one-character prefixes and twelve characters fell from 202 ms to 16 ms. 16 ms is the smallest wait the timer can show on Windows, and a search for a word in 0.1% of traces showed 11 ms on either thread. The thread adds 0.3 to 1.0 ms to a search: a word in 0.1% of traces took 4.8 ms against 4.0 on the server's thread, and 8.6 against 8.2 with CJK text. Its answers are the same as a search on the server's own connection; tests compare them across sort orders, pages, filters, CJK, and without FTS5. If the thread fails, the search it was running fails with the reason, and the next search starts a new thread. If the thread cannot start, searches run on the server's thread instead: the server logs the reason once, `/health` reports it under `search_worker` (`unavailable`, with the reason), and `--self-test` prints it. If the thread does not answer within the budget plus 10 s, the search answers as stopped with nothing read and the thread is replaced. Closing the store closes the thread's connection before its own, and waits at most 5 s for the thread: one inside a long statement cannot be stopped, so it is left to end when the statement does. A store in memory searches on its own connection.
- Searches that were already allowed cost about the same. Measured on 100,000 traces with main and this change in one process, alternating, median of 7: a word in every trace 208 ms against 246, sorted by timestamp 347 against 398, a phrase in half the traces 84 against 123, one agent's traces 167 against 154, and sixteen words that match no trace together 14 against 9. The search without FTS5 now reads the traces by rowid rather than sorting the tenant's rows again for every batch it read: 2.1 s against 4.1 for a word in every trace at 100,000.
- An FTS5 prefix index (`prefix='3'`) was measured and not added. It made four broad three-letter prefixes 3 times faster (186 ms against 559 at 100,000 traces), but made the file 20% larger and each insert 31% slower, for every trace, while the limits already hold those queries under the budget.
- Tests: the review's queries and 60 generated ones on a store shaped like the review's (every word starts with w), each on the index and on the search without FTS5, each refused or answered within a bound on CPU time; before this change, 8 repeats of `w*` on that store used 23.5 s of CPU. The budget is tested for which traces it keeps and how it ranks them, on both paths, and for the CPU time the search without FTS5 uses against reading everything.

**`delete_trace` no longer leaves the deleted text readable in `iris.db` (#703).** The database zeroes the pages a delete frees, but in write-ahead-log mode the zeroed pages go to `iris.db-wal`, and `iris.db` kept the old ones, with the trace's text, until the next checkpoint: for as long as the process ran. The retention sweep and `--purge` already checkpointed after deleting; `delete_trace` now does too, before it returns. Tests read the bytes of `iris.db` and `iris.db-wal` straight after the delete, for Latin text and for Chinese text and the two-character pieces the index keeps of it, and for a trace written since the last checkpoint. Each failed before the change. A delete takes longer: 24 ms against 15 at 100,000 traces, median of 20. A trace carrying an agent loop's spans takes 85 to 100 ms: taking a trace's words out of the search index grows with how many different words it holds. The API reference's `delete_trace` section states the cost. The checkpoint does not wait for a search that is reading the file, because waiting held the event loop for the rest of that search (470 to 620 ms at 100,000 traces). It is tried again every 20 ms until the reader finishes, so the text leaves the file then; a test deletes a trace while a search reads and checks the file's bytes once the search has finished.
- When a test finds a swept trace's word still in `iris.db`, its message now names the page of the file that holds it, the page's b-tree type, whether the file's free list names it, the connection's `secure_delete` and free-page count, and the rows of merge the sweep still owes. The test failed once on a hosted Windows runner with the word whole in `iris.db` and the log empty, and did not repeat in 50 local runs (#758).

**Revoking an API key takes effect on the next request, with no restart.** Remove a key from `security.apiKeys` in `config.json`, or delete its key file, and the next request with it is refused on the MCP transport and the dashboard alike. Every browser session it opened is signed out at the same moment, and other keys and their sessions carry on. Before, a leaked key kept working until the server restarted. On each request the server checks `config.json` and every key file it names with a few `stat` calls, and re-reads the keys only when one has changed: in a unit test, 50 requests with the files unchanged read `config.json` 0 times, and 50 after one edit read it once. Deleting one key's file revokes that key alone. A `config.json` that cannot be read fails closed: until it is fixed, only a key from `IRIS_API_KEY` or `--api-key` is accepted, and the log says why. A new `expiresAt` also applies without a restart. Proven through the real CLI: with a server serving both ports, rewriting `config.json` without a key refuses that key's next request with 403 on both ports, and its session's next request gets 401; the same test fails, with the revoked key still answered 200, when the server uses the old key ring. The key in `IRIS_API_KEY` or `--api-key`, and whether authentication is on at all, still change only on a restart.

**A browser session ends when the API key it signed in with expires.** Each dashboard session now records the key it was opened with and checks that key on every request, so a key past its `expiresAt`, or one no longer configured, signs its browsers out at the same moment the Bearer check starts refusing it. The session and its cookie's `Max-Age` are also capped at the key's expiry. Before, a browser signed in with an expiring key kept full access for up to 30 days. Proven through the real dashboard: a session opened with a key expiring in one hour answers 401 one hour and one second later, while a session from a key with no expiry is unaffected.

**The Python client is published only from a tag on `main`, built with hash-pinned tools.** `publish-python.yml` now refuses a `py-v*` tag whose commit is not on `main`, as `release.yml` does for `v*`. It installs `build` and the `hatchling` backend, with their 6 dependencies, from `.github/requirements/build.txt`, where every file is pinned by SHA-256 (`pip install --require-hashes --only-binary :all:`). It then builds with `--no-isolation`, so the build no longer downloads an unpinned backend. `build.txt` is generated from `build.in` with `pip-compile --generate-hashes` in `python:3.12-slim`, and Dependabot watches it.

**The SDK, the LangChain.js handler and the `iris-eval` launcher can be published by the release workflow, with npm provenance, once each is set up on npm.** A package joins a release when the workflow can publish it: its trusted publisher (this repository, `release.yml`) set on npmjs.com, or for its first version a one-time token stored, as `RELEASED_WITH_SERVER` in `scripts/claims/packages.mjs` records. None is yet, so this release publishes the server alone, and a package the workflow cannot publish no longer fails the run after the server is public. Two new release jobs handle them. `build-packages` runs with no publishing identity: it checks the packages (`scripts/check-npm-packages.mjs`), builds and typechecks them, and packs them. `publish-packages` runs only npm: it publishes each tarball whose version is new, in dependency order, after the server, with `--provenance`. `verify-release` then checks from outside that each package's version is on npm with an SLSA provenance statement. Each package's `publishConfig` requires provenance, so a publish from a machine that cannot attest its build is refused. `@iris-eval/sdk` and `@iris-eval/langchain` are no longer `private`. The launcher is at 1.0.1 in this repository, the same launcher with provenance once the workflow publishes it; 1.0.0, on npm, was published by hand without provenance and works the same. The release page carries these notes whole when they fit and, when they do not, everything before the first `###` heading whole with each later entry by its lead sentence and a link to the rest; `validate` refuses a tag whose notes do not fit even so, and `verify-release` checks that the page ends with the supply-chain block and the list of merged pull requests.

**CI installs the MCP clients it tests against from a lockfile.** Claude Code 2.1.282 and Gemini CLI 0.61.0 come from `.github/real-clients/package-lock.json` with `npm ci`, every package pinned by integrity hash, on Linux, macOS and Windows. Before, they came from `npm install -g`. Dependabot proposes client upgrades.

**`SECURITY.md` covers everything the repository publishes:** the container image, the MCPB bundle, the launcher, the JavaScript SDK, the LangChain.js handler, the Python client and the CI gate action, as well as the server, the dashboard and the website. Its self-hosting advice, and the README's data-on-disk section, now recommend encrypting the disk or volume that holds the Iris home. Iris does not encrypt at rest: its database files are owner-only, and it stores no LLM provider keys.

**The storage threads start from fixed code.** Run from its TypeScript sources (its tests, `npx tsx`), Iris used to start the search and checkpoint threads from code with the entry file's URL written into it. They now start from one constant and receive the URL as an argument (`src/storage/source-thread.ts`), which closes two CodeQL `js/bad-code-sanitization` alerts. The published package never took this path: it starts the compiled worker files directly.

sections.title: Added
items: **`state` on every rule result, bundle row, run result and case attempt, and a count of what was not checked beside every pass count.** A rule result carries `state` (`pass`, `fail`, `not_checked`): a rule that skipped still carries `passed: false` and `score: 0` as placeholders, and `state` is what to read. A rule that skipped for missing evidence carries `lacked` (the inputs it reads that the call did not carry) and, when somebody had asked for it, `asked` (`config` or `call`). `GET /api/v1/runs/:id` and `GET /api/v1/cases/:key` carry `state` on each row; `GET /api/v1/runs`, the case route, `GET /api/v1/eval-stats`, each drift window, the summary (`eval_not_checked`), `compare_runs` and `evaluate_runs` (`not_checked`) say how many verdicts were not checked. Pass rates keep those in the denominator, so leaving out what a check reads never raises a rate. The dashboard draws such a verdict as NOT CHECKED in grey where it drew a red FAIL, says "2 not checked" beside the counts, and its result filter reads "Did not pass". The recent-failures list leaves such verdicts out and names the rule that decided, and the count of leaks no longer counts a `no_pii` that skipped. The gate action's receipt has a Verdict column (failed, or not checked). Migration `021-eval-verdict-state` adds the column the counts read; rows from earlier releases are filled in the background after the first start and are counted as before until then, and a stored row that cannot be read no longer stops that background step at itself.

**`verdict_not_checked` webhook event**, for a verdict that was not checked and that no layer failed, with the missing input or the check that could not answer as its subject. An alert on `verdict_fail` alone stayed silent when an agent stopped sending the evidence a check reads.

**`proof/INVARIANTS.md`: what a verdict does when evidence is left out, and when a failure is added.** `npm run proof -- --invariants` takes each of the 145 labelled cases, sends the call without one field at a time (deleted, or a blank in its place) and counts the verdicts that got better, then adds one more failure to each and counts the ones rescued by it. With nothing said about what a call must carry the counts are not zero and are published as they are: of 72 failing cases that carry tool calls, 39 pass when the calls are left out. Where a contract is in force (the deployment requires the input, the deployment set the threshold of a rule that reads it, or the call supplied what it is compared with) no case passes with the field left out, and none of five fixed additions rescues a case; CI holds both at zero. **Decision Moments can be ranked by significance, and the Moments page ranks by default (#409).** Newest first put a safety violation behind every trace that came after it. `GET /api/v1/moments?sort_by=significance` reads the newest `window` traces that match the agent and time filters (default and maximum 500), classifies each, applies the verdict and significance filters, and ranks them: `significance.score` descending, then newest first, then trace id. Pages are cut from that one ranking, so `total` is exact within the window and page two begins where page one ended. The response states the window it read (`window.size`, `scanned`, `tracesInRange`, `newest`, `oldest`), and passing `until` = `window.newest` keeps later pages on the same ranking while traces arrive. The significance tiers, most serious first, are severity (a safety or veto rule failed, 1.0), change against the agent's own baseline (cost spike 0.9, regression alarm 0.85), and rarity (first failure 0.8, new combination 0.75), then the ordinary outcomes; `docs/api-reference.md` has the table and the history each class needs. On a 240-trace fixture with a safety violation, a cost spike and a first failure, newest first shows them at positions 210, 150 and 90, and the ranking shows them at 1, 2 and 3. A 500-trace window over a 2,000-trace store answers in a median 334 ms locally, against 66 ms for a newest-first page of 50. The Moments page asks for the ranking by default, polls it every 10 seconds instead of 3, says how far back it reached ("Ranked by significance within the last 500 traces of 1,200 …"), and offers Newest first as an order (`?sort=newest`). `sort_by` defaults to `timestamp`, so existing callers are unchanged. A `window` without `sort_by=significance`, or `sort_order=asc` with it, is refused with a 400 rather than ignored.

**An off-topic answer fails when you turn on the relevance judge (#649).** Set `IRIS_RELEVANCE_JUDGE_MODEL` to a priced model id, with that provider's key, and `answers_the_ask` asks a new `relevance` judge template whether the output addresses its ask. It then gates on the judge's verdict: an off-topic answer fails with `verdict.basis: "policy_gate"` and `verdict.by: ["answers_the_ask"]`. A correct paraphrase that shares none of the ask's words passes, and a one-word answer or a one-term ask is judged rather than skipped. That is one judge call per evaluation that carries an input, on `evaluate_output`, `log_trace` with `evaluate: true`, HTTP and OTLP ingest, `iris-eval ingest` and `evaluate_runs` alike, capped by `IRIS_LLM_JUDGE_MAX_COST_USD_PER_EVAL`. A provider key alone never turns it on. The rule's result carries `kind: "judgment"`, `role: "gate"`, the judge's score against its 0.60 pass line, its rationale and what the call cost. When the judge cannot answer (an unpriced model, no key, the cost cap, a provider error), the result records why, the rule falls back to its lexical reading, which advises, and `interpretations` says so. A judge from the agent's own model family still decides, with the same-family warning in `interpretations`. Installing a judge changes the ruleset hash, so `evaluate_runs` re-scores traces judged without it. `iris://capabilities` → `judge.relevance` and `--self-test` show whether it is on and whether it can be called. Embedders install it with `engine.setRelevanceJudge(createRelevanceJudge({ model, apiKey }))`.

**The `relevance` judge template, for `evaluate_with_llm_judge` too.** It asks whether the output addresses this request rather than another subject or question, and it does not judge correctness or helpfulness: a wrong answer to the question asked is relevant. It scores against five anchored points with a 0.60 pass line, requires `input` (refused with `IRIS_INVALID_ARGUMENT` before any spend), and returns `addresses_request`, `on_subject` and `specific_to_request`. It wraps the request and the output in the per-call nonce tags, and it tells the judge to score an instruction aimed at itself as absent. A new template, so no existing score shifts. Its proof set is 36 labelled cases in `proof/judge/cases/relevance.json`: 18 that should pass, 9 of them shaped to fool word matching; 12 violations; and 6 injection twins. `npm run proof:judge` also measures `answers_the_ask` with the judge installed on the rule's own 45-case corpus family, beside the lexical rule. It then measures the whole composite verdict with the judge installed, on the test, dev and real-transcript splits, beside the same corpus without it. All three need a key and are pending until a keyed run is published. The composite harness now gates on a judgment as the product's composer does, so that measurement is of the composer the product runs. It is proved without a key on a stand-in judge that fails everything: the four off-task composite cases the shipped config lets through then fail. What CI measures without a key: on those 36 cases the lexical `answers_the_ask` fails 10 of the 18 it should fail and wrongly fails 2 of the 18 it should pass. One relevance judgment's worst case is $0.0060 on `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` and $0.0008 on `gpt-4o-mini`.

**The relevance judge spends within a daily budget, keeps personal data and credentials from the provider, and says when it reaches the network (#649).** With `IRIS_RELEVANCE_JUDGE_MODEL` set, every evaluation that carries an input makes a judge call on your key, and the provider wrappers ask for evaluation on every call they record. Until this change only each call was capped; nothing capped the total, and the ask and the answer went to the provider exactly as they were.
- `IRIS_RELEVANCE_JUDGE_DAILY_BUDGET_USD`, default 1, is what the judge may spend per UTC day, per tenant. It is kept in the database (migration 017, table `relevance_judge_spend`), so a restart, a second server on the same file and `iris-eval ingest` draw on one balance. A call is made only if its worst case, priced as the per-call cap prices it, fits in what is left. The worst case is replaced by the actual cost when the call returns, so the day's total never passes the budget. At the $0.0060 worst case above, the default admits at least 165 judgments a day. Past it, `answers_the_ask` reads the ask lexically, `judge.withheld` is `daily_budget` with the reason in `judge.error`, and the server logs one warning line per tenant per day (once per process). `0` stops every call.
- `IRIS_RELEVANCE_JUDGE_MAX_CALLS_PER_REQUEST`, default 20, caps judge calls in one request. An OTLP request of up to 2,000 traces, or an `evaluate_runs` re-score of a whole run, judges its first 20 and reads the rest lexically with `judge.withheld: "request_cap"`. The OTLP answer carries `iris-eval.relevance_judge: { calls, withheld, max_calls_per_request }`, and the `evaluate_runs` summary says how many were withheld.
- Before a call, every span Iris's own `no_pii` rule flags in the input and the output is replaced by a numbered marker such as `[REDACTED:Email#1]`. That covers the personal-data patterns, the API keys and tokens, private key blocks, seed phrases, and any of those inside a base64 run. It uses the rule's detector, not a second list, and every match is replaced, not only the 25 the rule keeps as evidence. A value that appears in both texts gets one marker, and the prompt tells the judge to read a marker as the value it replaced. `judge.redacted` counts the replacements. `IRIS_RELEVANCE_JUDGE_REDACT=off` sends the text as it is and marks each record `sentUnredacted: true`. Redaction is on by default because relevance is about the subject, not the digits of a card number.
- The README, `docs/llm-as-judge.md` and the enable steps say what leaves the machine: the evaluation's input and output, to Anthropic or OpenAI, on your key, and nothing else from the trace.
- With a relevance judge installed, `evaluate_output`, `log_trace` and `evaluate_runs` advertise `openWorldHint: true`, and `evaluate_output` advertises `idempotentHint: false`. Without one they are unchanged.
- `iris://capabilities` → `judge.relevance` carries `egress`, `redact`, `maxCallsPerRequest` and today's `budget` (spent, remaining, calls, refused, when it resets). `--self-test` prints the same line, with today's spend read from the install's database. `GET /api/v1/health` carries `judge.relevance.budget_exhausted`. It does not report the amount, since the endpoint answers without a key.
- A relevance judge that is configured and cannot run (no key for its provider, or an unpriced model) no longer fails silently. The server and `iris-eval ingest` print one warning line at startup naming what is missing, and `--self-test` fails its judge step and exits 1 instead of printing PASS. Each result still carries `judge.error` and the lexical reading.
- The Claude Desktop bundle (`iris-eval.mcpb`) asks for a relevance judge model (optional, empty by default) and the daily budget (default 1), beside the two provider keys, which stay masked. Its description says what naming a model sends.
- Proven end to end with the provider replaced at `fetch`, so the tests read the request body that would go out: `tests/integration/relevance-judge-limits.test.ts`, `tests/unit/eval/llm-judge/judge-budget.test.ts` and `tests/unit/eval/llm-judge/redact.test.ts`.

**Full-text search over traces: find the run where the agent said it** (#7). `get_traces`, `GET /api/v1/traces` and the Python client's `get_traces()` take `q`, and the dashboard's trace list has a search box. It searches each trace's input, output, and the values in its tool calls and metadata (never their keys). Every word must appear; `"a phrase"` matches in order; `word*` is a prefix; case and accents are ignored. Results are ranked by relevance (BM25) unless `sort_by` says otherwise, the other filters still apply, and each trace carries `match`: the field it matched in, a snippet, and the snippet as fragments with the matched words marked. Anything typed is read as words, never as SQLite query syntax: `NEAR(`, `OR`, `input:`, stray quotes and parentheses cannot fail or widen a search (a property test runs 400 generated hostile queries per driver and requires the index and a plain read of the traces to return the same traces). A `q` with no letter or digit is refused with a message rather than answered with an empty page.
- The index is an SQLite FTS5 table in the same file, holding no second copy of the text (except, for a trace with Chinese, Japanese or Korean in it, the pieces its CJK text is indexed as: see the entry for words inside CJK text). Migration 015 creates it empty and the server indexes the traces already stored in the background after it starts, and builds the covering index a search's filters read after the start as well; a batch of 100 traces or more is indexed in the transaction that writes it, and a smaller one is queued there and indexed in batches after it (a search indexes the queue first, so it misses nothing just stored), and triggers take a trace out on every delete and update, including the retention sweep, `--purge` and a DELETE run by hand. A deleted trace's words are removed from the index as well as its row: tests delete a trace, run a sweep and a purge, checkpoint, and find none of the removed words in `iris.db` or `iris.db-wal`.
- better-sqlite3's SQLite has FTS5; Node's built-in `node:sqlite` has it from Node 22.16.0, not on 22.13.0 to 22.15.0. On a SQLite without FTS5, search still works by reading the traces with the same matching (slower; `search.index` says `scan`), and the index is built on the first start that has FTS5. A new CI job checks both drivers on Linux, macOS and Windows, the built-in at Node 22.13.0 (the scan, on a real SQLite without FTS5) and 24.
- Measured with `npx tsx scripts/bench-trace-search.ts` on an Intel Core i9-12900HK laptop (20 threads, 32 GB, Windows 11), Node 24.11.0, better-sqlite3 with SQLite 3.53.2, synthetic traces of about 140 words each, a page of 50 with the total counted, median of 15 runs. At 10,000 traces: 1.3 ms for a word in 0.1% of traces, 4.7 ms for one in 10%, 33.7 ms for one in every trace. At 100,000 traces: 3.1 ms, 35.6 ms and 258.5 ms; 9.0 ms for a word in 1% of traces and 168.8 ms for a phrase in half of them. The same queries without the index took 8 to 14 s at 100,000 traces.
- What it costs, from the same run: at 100,000 traces the file grows from 125 MB to 211 MB, an insert takes 364 µs per trace instead of 149 µs, deleting one trace takes 14.5 ms, and a retention sweep of 3,007 traces 4.3 s. Building the index for 100,000 existing traces took 8.5 s in the background, measured separately with the server started in 228 ms (an integration test starts the real server over stdio on 40,000 unindexed traces and gets an answer, and a correct search, before the index is ready).
- The dashboard's clickable table rows are no longer themselves buttons: a row opens on a click anywhere and from a named button in its first cell, so the copy-id button inside a trace row is reachable by keyboard and screen reader (axe reported it as nested-interactive).

**Search reads what a trace's spans say: the later model calls, tool results and exceptions of an agent loop sent over OTLP (#683).** A trace from `POST /v1/traces`, which is how the provider wrappers and LangChain send, keeps only its first model call's input and output on the trace row; the rest was only in its spans, so a word from the third model call, a tool result or an exception message found nothing. `q` now also searches `spans`: the string values of each span's attributes and of its events' attributes, in span start order.
- Never keys, numbers or booleans, and not the `otel.span_id` and `otel.parent_span_id` attributes Iris adds. A string that holds JSON, such as `gen_ai.input.messages`, is read by the strings inside it, so `role` and `content` are not words of every trace. Each distinct string is indexed once per trace, so the conversation history every model call re-sends adds nothing. At most 4,096 characters of one value and 32,768 of one trace's span text are indexed: words past either cap are not searchable.
- `match.field` is `spans` for a match there, and `match.span` names the span (`span_id`, `name`); the dashboard shows the span's name beside the excerpt. Span text is weighted like tool-call and metadata values (half of `input` and `output`).
- Deletes stay exact. The span text is computed in SQL from the spans table by every write and every trigger, and no copy of it is stored; a trace's words leave the index before its spans are deleted with it, and a span inserted, changed or deleted after its trace was indexed (by `insertSpan`, or by hand) re-indexes the trace. Tests check FTS5's own integrity check after each of those, and that a deleted trace's span words are not left in `iris.db` or its WAL.
- Found on both SQLite drivers, and without FTS5, where the search reads the traces and reads a trace's span text only when its own fields lack a word and its stored span JSON could hold it.
- What it costs, measured on the benchmark machine with the code before this change and after it run side by side in one process, each step alternated, on traces that are each an agent loop of three model calls and two tool calls:
| | 10,000 traces, before | 10,000, after | 100,000, before | 100,000, after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| File | 84 MB | 102 MB | 841 MB | 993 MB |
| The index in it | 7.7 MB | 23.0 MB | 73.4 MB | 225.1 MB |
| Insert, per trace | 493 µs | 1,320 µs | 564 µs | 1,675 µs |
| `delete_trace`, median of 20 | 18.3 ms | 73.7 ms | 27.3 ms | 118.3 ms |
| Retention sweep of 3% | 0.46 s | 1.30 s | 6.7 s | 22.9 s |
| Search, a word in 1% of outputs | 4.1 ms | 7.7 ms | 8.7 ms | 12.0 ms |
| Search, a word only in spans (1% of traces) | not found | 21.4 ms | not found | 28.3 ms |
| Without FTS5, a word in 1% of outputs | 625 ms | 2,271 ms | 10.7 s | 23.5 s |
| Without FTS5, a word only in spans | not found | 1,406 ms | not found | 36.0 s |
The retention sweep row is how long the sweep takes; it now runs in the background, in steps, after the server answers (see Check before upgrading).
Without FTS5 (and while the index is being built) a search reads the traces, and now reads span text too, for the traces whose own fields lack a word and whose stored spans could hold it: two to four times as long. Traces without spans cost the same as before: at 100,000, 211 MB either way, 317 µs per insert against 308, and `delete_trace` 14.7 ms against 15.2.

**A word inside Chinese, Japanese or Korean text is found (#682).** Those languages put no spaces between words, and the index kept a run of CJK characters as one word, so `批准` ("approved") did not find `退款已经批准了`; only the whole run did.
