A field that holds CJK is now also indexed as the overlapping two-character pieces of each run, and a CJK search word is cut the same way and searched as those pieces in order. A word of one, two or more characters is found anywhere inside a run, in order and within one run (`批准了请` does not match across the comma in `批准了，请`), with the index and without FTS5, and the snippet marks the matched characters inside the run. Latin written against CJK is a word of its own there (`iphone` finds `iPhone充电器`).
- Search now splits text exactly as the index does. It used to approximate SQLite's tokenizer, which split Korean syllables into letters: a Korean word searched with the index found nothing, while the same search without FTS5 found it. The split is now read from a table of what SQLite's `unicode61` tokenizer does with each of the 1,112,063 code points, generated from SQLite by `npm run unicode61:render`; a CI job regenerates it and fails when it differs, and a test checks 2,000 random strings drawn from Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hangul, kana, Han, emoji, private-use characters and combining marks against FTS5 itself.
- Traces without CJK cost the same as before, measured with the code before this change and after it run side by side in one process, each step alternated, on traces that are each an agent loop of three model calls and two tool calls. At 10,000 traces: 1,410 µs per insert against 1,388, 102 MB either way, and a search for a word in 1% of traces 3.3 ms against 6.6 (the snippet's word split is faster now). At 100,000: 1,871 µs per insert against 1,793, 993 MB either way, `delete_trace` 276 ms against 268, a 3% retention sweep 24.8 s against 22.9 (an earlier run of this change came out the other way on each, by as much: the machine's own variation). With accented Latin text: 1,968 µs per insert against 1,877, and 130 MB either way. Their words never enter the CJK tables.
- What CJK text costs, on the same agent loops written in Chinese, at 10,000 traces:
| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| File | 128 MB | 251 MB |
| Insert, per trace | 1,936 µs | 6,622 µs |
| `delete_trace`, median of 20 | 24.5 ms | 244.9 ms |
| Retention sweep of 3% | 1.96 s | 4.89 s |
| Search, a CJK word inside a run (1% of traces) | not found | 28.5 ms |
| Search, a Latin word in every trace | 54.6 ms | 86.6 ms |
| Without FTS5, a Latin word in 1% of traces | 4.2 s | 6.9 s |
| Index built after upgrading from 0.19.0 | 7.4 s | 50.8 s |
Every CJK character is a word of the index twice over (in two pieces), and each is erased from the index when its trace is deleted, which is where the file size and the delete time go.
- **A trace with CJK text keeps a second, derived copy of that text in the file: the pieces its CJK is indexed as.** The rest of the index holds no copy of any trace's text; SQLite recomputes what a delete must hand the index from the trace row itself. The pieces are cut by JavaScript, which a trigger cannot run, so the text each trace's pieces were given is stored beside them, and every delete hands it back. That copy leaves the file with the trace on every route: `delete_trace`, the retention sweep, `--purge`, a `DELETE` run by hand, and the metadata patch when it replaces the text. Its pages are zeroed as the trace's row is. Tests check the file's bytes after each route: none of the deleted trace's CJK pieces is left in `iris.db` or its WAL. A trace without CJK has no such copy.

**Every verdict says who recorded what it judged, and a capture harness can certify that no tool was called.** An empty list of tool calls says two different things: from software that watched the agent and records every call, that none were made; from the agent's own report, only that it reported none, which an agent that hid a failed call can say as easily as one that made no call. A capture source now declares itself on the trace: `capture: { name, version, complete }` on `POST /api/v1/traces` and `iris-eval ingest`, or `iris.capture.name`, `iris.capture.version` and `iris.capture.complete` on an OTLP resource, where `complete` lists what it records in full (`input`, `tool_calls`, `tool_outputs`; over OTLP `input` and `tool_outputs` only, since one trace can arrive in several requests and a request without a TOOL span cannot show that none was made). Its empty list of tool calls is then evidence that no tool was called: it meets `eval.requiredEvidence: ["tool_calls"]`, and the verdict's coverage says "no tool was called". A field it declares and the trace leaves out is a hole in the record, and the verdict is `unknown` (`required_evidence_missing`), with a sentence to the operator naming the capture source and the field; on the labelled corpus, leaving a declared field out never yields a pass (`proof/INVARIANTS.md`, four held rows). `log_trace` takes no `capture`, since the agent calls it and a record cannot vouch for itself. Each evaluation carries `provenance.evidence`: `recordedBy` (`harness`, `agent`, `not_declared`), the capture source, the inputs the call carried, and how many tool calls it carried; a stored evaluation reads back with the same, a trace scored again by its id is judged on the declaration it was stored with, and the dashboard's verdict panel says who recorded the evidence. The Claude Code capture plugin declares itself on every turn, and declares complete only what that part of the turn holds. Iris cannot check a declaration, as it cannot check the calls themselves: the contract says who made each claim, so a deployment can decide which sources it trusts. [The evidence contract](docs/api-reference.md#the-evidence-contract-who-recorded-the-trace).

sections.title: Changed
items: **`provenance.composer.calibration` names the calibration table, not the corpus it was measured on.** The table behind the confidence label (`src/eval/published-calibration.ts`) is regenerated whenever a rule moves a verdict, while the composite corpus stays the same, so a stamp of the corpus's version would let a later table label a stored verdict again. The table now carries its own version, a hash over its content, and verdicts are stamped with it; a stored verdict is labelled again only under the table it was given with. Rows written by 0.19.0 already read back without a label, and still do. `proof/COMPOSITE.md` adds the AUC beside Brier and ECE: the chance a bad output gets a higher estimate than a good one, which does not move when every estimate moves.

**The published verdict accuracy is measured through the composer the server runs.** The composite table was scored by a second composer kept in the harness, which agreed with the server's on every case and would have kept publishing its own answer if the two had drifted. The harness now calls `compose()`, a test holds that the verdict scored on each case is the one the engine gave, and the second composer is removed. `proof/COMPOSITE.md` also counts the three states apart, so a verdict that was not checked is never folded into the blocks or the passes. No published number changed.

**A Decision Moment whose trace has one passing evaluation and one that was not checked reads "No verdict".** It read `pass`: the evaluation that could not be reached was dropped before the count. Its reason now names all three ways a verdict is not reached, where it named two.

**The 24 real transcripts: bundle verdicts agreeing with the answer key went from 78 to 82 of 96**, and transcripts whose four bundles all agree from 11 to 13, because a bundle row is now the verdict read for its rules. Five recorded gaps closed and one opened (the placeholder detector lives in the safety bundle, and the answer key files a deferral under completeness); `proof/TRANSCRIPTS.md` lists each.

**iris-eval.com shows what exists today: the open-source server.** The home page and the pricing page show it alone; hosted and team features are under consideration, not under construction. The planned hosted plans shown beside it, the waitlist form and the "Join Cloud Waitlist" button in the hero are removed; several features those plans listed were already in the open-source server. The signup route (`POST /api/waitlist` on the site) is removed and `/waitlist` redirects to `/pricing`. The terms' section for a future paid service is removed. The security page says Iris is self-hosted today, that none of your traces reach us, that Iris holds no certification and that tenant isolation is already enforced in the storage code, with what exists today and what does not, in place of "pre-SOC-2" and "enterprise customers". The privacy policy says the form is removed, that an address given while it was open is still held and is deleted on request, and that text pasted into the playground is scored and returned without being stored. The repository's sponsor link, which pointed at the waitlist, is removed.
**Community links point to GitHub, npm and X.** The footer and the home page's community section list the places Iris is active; the "Discord (coming soon)" entry is removed.

**Iris's own test runs stay out of its public download count.** The upgrade test takes the previous release's tarball from a cache and fetches it from the npm registry only on a cache miss. It used to install from the registry on every run, on three operating systems, and those installs were most of what the package's download count measured. The test installs the tarball it is given, refuses a missing one rather than falling back to the registry, and checks the version it installed. The total-downloads badge, whose all-time number includes those runs, is removed from the README and the site.

**Background work's steps are sized to stay under 50 ms, and the index build no longer runs FTS5's merges inside them.** Each step of the index build, the retention sweep, the merge a sweep owes, the erasure of a retired index and the fill of stored risk estimates after an upgrade is now sized to 35 ms, from the work the last step did and how long it took, its commit included. A step grows by at most half the last one, so the next step has room before the 50 ms bound. The index build also turns FTS5's automerge off inside its own steps. Automerge had merged older segments inside whichever step's commit flushed, and those were the build's slowest steps. The build now merges the index's levels in steps of their own. Those merge steps are sized by the rows each one wrote, never by a budget it left unused, and capped at 512 pages, past which one merge's work comes in lumps. Measured on the benchmark machine against the code before this change, alternated, at 100,000 agent-loop traces, while other work shared the machine. A hold is read as this thread's CPU time, so time the process spent waiting to be scheduled is not counted.
- Over stdio, the longest hold after the first answer was 78 and 62 ms instead of 125 and 126 ms while the index was built after an upgrade from 0.19.0. It was 78 and 64 ms instead of 125 and 126 ms while a retired index was erased and the index rebuilt, and 78 and 78 ms instead of 94 and 93 ms during a retention sweep of 3,000 traces. At 10,000 traces the build's longest hold was 48 to 63 ms instead of 94 to 109 ms; the sweep's did not improve (62 to 79 ms against 63 ms).
- In one process, the build after an upgrade had 2 and 3 steps over 50 ms instead of 536 and 584, and took 70.4 and 70.7 s against 71.2 and 75.7 s. The sweep had 6 and 7 instead of 33 and 35. The rebuild after a retired index had 32 and 39 instead of 655 and 752, measured while the machine was busier.
- The fill of stored risk estimates after an upgrade from 0.19.0 with 20,000 evaluations stopped each step at 50 ms of estimates and then committed, and the commit rewrote every row the step touched: 349 of 351 steps held the event loop over 50 ms, with 62 to 78 ms of this thread's CPU at the median. Sized with its commit, 45 of 644 steps did, and a step took 31 ms of CPU at the median (both drivers, two runs each).

**After upgrading, the server answers its client before it copies and migrates the database.** The copy taken before a migration and the migrations themselves ran before the MCP connection opened, on the event loop: from 0.19.0 at 100,000 agent-loop traces, the first answer (`initialize`) came 5.0 to 7.3 s after the server started (six runs over stdio, median 6.7 s). The server now answers first, in 0.68 to 1.02 s (median 0.82 s), and copies and migrates after, on the checkpoint worker's connection, so neither holds the event loop: the copy is finished before the first migration writes, and nothing else writes until both are done. A tool call, a resource read or an HTTP request that arrives meanwhile waits for them, at most 30 s, and is then refused with a sentence saying what the server is doing (`IRIS_STORAGE_ERROR`, retryable; HTTP 503 with `Retry-After`); it is never answered from the older schema. The bound is for large files: the 790 MB file of 100,000 agent-loop traces copied in 3.5 s, so at that rate a million traces would take about 35 s to copy alone, and a request arriving then is refused with the reason rather than left waiting. The first `get_traces` call, sent right after `initialize`, still waits for the copy and the migrations: it was answered 6.2 to 7.8 s after the start (median 7.1 s), against 5.0 to 7.3 s (median 6.7 s) when both ran before the connection opened, so running them on the worker's connection costs about 0.4 s at the median on this first call after an upgrade. `GET /health` answers throughout, and its new `upgrade` field says whether the store is copying or migrating, or why the upgrade failed. The deployment's verdict labels are read before any request is let through, as they were before the connection opened. The stall guard now runs an upgrade from 0.19.0 at 10,000 traces, the start included: its longest hold was 48 ms, and 421 ms with the copy and the migrations back on the event loop. `iris-eval ingest`, `--purge`, `--self-test` and an embedder's `initialize()` still return with the file migrated; `upgradeAfterStart` on the adapter's options is what the server sets.

**After upgrading, the server answers before the covering index for search filters is built.** Migration 015 built `idx_traces_search_filter` before the MCP connection opened, in one statement that reads every trace row. The server now builds it after the start, on the checkpoint worker's own connection, so the event loop stays free while it runs. It logs `Search index: the covering index for search filters was built after the start, in N s` when it is done. Until then a search is correct, and slower, because it joins through the traces' own key. The index holds the write lock while it builds: the store's own background work waits for it, and a trace written in that moment waits for it too, as it would behind any other writer. Measured in one process at 100,000 agent-loop traces from 0.19.0, the start, migrations included, took 1.87 and 2.23 s instead of 2.41 and 2.53 s; the index is 0.62 to 0.68 s of that. The rest of the start is migration 019's indexes: 1.69 to 1.87 s.

**Each connection compiles a statement once (#711).** Both drivers keep what they prepare, up to 256 statements, and drop the least recently used first. A kept statement stays correct when the schema changes under it, including when another process changes it. Before this, every call compiled its SQL again, and with the search index that was most of a write: compiling the insert into `spans` compiles six triggers. `log_trace` over stdio takes 1.29 ms at 10,000 traces and 1.34 ms at 100,000 (2.25 and 2.34 ms without the cache, and 0.99 and 0.96 ms in 0.19.0). What still separates it from 0.19.0 is the search index's own write: a stored trace writes 38 pages to the log where 0.19.0 wrote 13.5.

**Storing one trace no longer writes the search index in the same commit (#729).** `log_trace` and `POST /api/v1/traces` store the trace and queue its id. Indexing a trace on its own took 558 µs; in a batch of 1,000 it takes 95 µs. The queue is indexed when writes pause for 25 ms, in steps of about 35 ms under their own write lock, with FTS5's merges in steps of their own. During a stream of writes it is indexed only once this process has queued 1,000 traces, and a write that finds more queued indexes some of it first, so the queue never holds more. A batch of 100 traces or more (an OTLP request, `iris-eval ingest`) is indexed in the transaction that stores it, as before, because it is already a batch. A search indexes the queue first, in the same steps with other requests answered between them, so it finds every trace stored before it and ranks exactly as before. At 100,000 traces, a search that first indexed 990 queued agent-loop traces answered in 594 to 623 ms, complete, and held the event loop for 65 ms at the longest, with a checkpoint running. No step starts while the checkpoint worker truncates the log, which holds the write lock. Every delete route takes a queued trace off the queue, and its text leaves the file as an indexed trace's does. Measured over stdio on the machine in #711, five alternated rounds of 200 `log_trace` calls sent back to back: at 10,000 traces the median is 1.22 ms and the 95th percentile 1.65 ms (without this change 1.72 and 4.72 ms; 0.19.0 1.02 and 2.46 ms), and at 100,000 traces 1.32 and 2.64 ms (without it 1.92 and 3.50; 0.19.0 1.25 and 2.13). In a stream of 2,000 back to back, where the queue passes 1,000 and is indexed between writes, the 95th percentile at 100,000 traces is 3.9 ms against 3.0 without this change, and the 99th 36 ms against 27. Sustained OTLP ingest is unchanged by it: 1,999 traces/s at 100,000 traces against 1,935 without it, and 2,054 at 10,000 against 2,057 (0.19.0, which had no index: 2,396 and 2,680).

**`GET /api/v1/health` and `GET /health` carry `search`: the index's `state` (`ready`, `building` or `unavailable`), `index` (what a search reads now, `fts5` or `scan`) and `progress`, the share of stored traces indexed, from 0 to 0.99 while it is built.** A share and not a count, because the endpoint answers without a key. It is not a check: a search answers in every state, so it never makes the status `degraded`. `--self-test` gains a line for the configured database's index (`ready: 100,000 trace(s) indexed`, or how many of how many, or that the SQLite has no FTS5), read without changing the file.

**GenAI message arrays are read down to their words, for every framework.** The words reader added for LangSmith's LangChain envelopes now reads `gen_ai.input.messages` / `gen_ai.output.messages` (the conventions' `parts` schema) and OpenAI's `[{ role, content }]` the same way. The rules judge the answer's words and search finds them: before, `?q=role` matched every GenAI trace and the rules read a JSON document. Proved per framework by the conventions fixtures (Pydantic AI, Semantic Kernel and LangSmith's documented shape change; the others already carried words), and through the OTLP door by one test that stores, searches and scores a message-array trace.

**The agent's own span is filed as the agent, not as a model call.** `invoke_agent` and `create_agent` spans map to `INTERNAL` whatever else they carry; before, any non-empty `gen_ai.operation.name` made a span `LLM`, so the Agent Framework's `invoke_agent` (which carries the model's name and the run's usage) showed as a third model call beside two real ones. Usage is summed over the leaf carriers whatever their kind, so the totals are unchanged: the Agent Framework, Google ADK and Pydantic AI fixtures keep 1,742/136, 318/44 and 812/133 tokens, and the door test reads the same totals from `GET /api/v1/traces/:id`.

**Installing Iris succeeds where `better-sqlite3` cannot be built (#661).** `better-sqlite3` moves from `dependencies` to `optionalDependencies`. On a platform with no prebuilt binary and no C++ toolchain, npm now prints the build error, skips the module and finishes the install, and Iris runs on Node's built-in SQLite (`node:sqlite`), which it already fell back to when the module could not load. The warning, the startup log and `--self-test` now say which driver holds the file and why: `better-sqlite3 loaded (the default)`, `IRIS_SQLITE_DRIVER=node chose Node's built-in SQLite`, `better-sqlite3 is not installed …`, or `better-sqlite3 could not load (<reason>) …`, and the advice differs (`npm install better-sqlite3` for an absent module, `npm rebuild better-sqlite3` for a broken one). A CI job installs the packed server into an empty project with the native build forced to fail (no prebuilt download, a compiler that always fails), requires the module to be absent and the install to finish, then requires `--self-test` to start the server, store a trace and read it back on `node:sqlite`, and `iris-eval ingest --evaluate` to store and score one more. The lockfile, regenerated on Linux, marks `better-sqlite3` and the 32 packages only it pulls in as optional, and the two it shares with development tooling (`detect-libc`, `semver`) as dev-optional; no version moved. The MCP bundle's packer (`scripts/mcpb/pack.mjs`) now walks the root's optional dependencies as well as its dependencies, so it still finds `better-sqlite3` and leaves it out by name.

**A filtered Decision Moments list returns full pages (#657).** `GET /api/v1/moments` in its default time order applied the `verdict`, `min_significance` and `significance_kind` filters after reading a page of traces: on one agent's 240 traces with a failure every twelfth, `?verdict=fail&limit=10` returned 1 moment, the next page returned 0, and `total` said 240, with 20 failures in the store. With a filter set, the route now reads a window, the first `window` traces (default and maximum 500) matching the agent and time filters in the order asked for, the way `sort_by=significance` does. It filters every moment in it and cuts pages from that list. The same query returns 10, then the other 10, with `total` 20, and the response states the window. The dashboard's Moments page says how far back a filtered list reached ("Filtered within the last 500 traces of 1,200 …"), the Stream view's list of significant moments asks for a 200-trace window, the number of traces it read on each poll before, and the recent-moments row beside it now reads 200 traces instead of 48, so it finds moments further back. Unfiltered reads are unchanged.

**The dashboard loads each page's code when the page is shown (#662).** Every page's code used to arrive in one bundle before the first page rendered: 576,945 bytes, 166,296 gzipped. Each page, and each of the four views of `/` (Failures, Health, Drift, Stream), is now its own chunk. The first load (the shell, the router, the design system and the data hooks the shell shares with the pages) is 308,822 bytes, 97,068 gzipped, and the default landing view needs 335,744 bytes, 109,015 gzipped, 34% less than before. The charting code Health and Drift share arrives only with them. Once the first page has rendered, the other pages' code is fetched while the browser is idle, so moving between pages does not wait on the network. A page whose code is still arriving shows "Loading page…" in a polite status region, visible only after 250 ms so a fast load does not flash, with the sidebar and header usable. A page whose code cannot be fetched, usually because Iris was upgraded while the tab stayed open, says so and offers a reload instead of the generic error. Hashed files under `/assets/` are now served as immutable for a year, so a reload does not re-request each chunk against the rate limit the dashboard's polling shares, and a missing asset is a 404 instead of the app's HTML. The bundle budget gate now reads Vite's build manifest and holds the first load to 350 KB raw and 110 KB gzipped, and every other chunk to a budget of its own (the shared d3 chunk 52 / 19 KB, any other chunk 28 / 10 KB); a named budget that matches no chunk fails the gate. Upgrading React to 19.3 measures at 605,618 bytes, 175,048 gzipped, as a single bundle, over the old 168 KB gzip budget; on top of this change its first load is 337,430 bytes, 105,353 gzipped, inside the new one.

**Behaviour change: `verify_citations` reports a judge failure under `judge_error`, not `resolve_error` (#407).** When a source resolved and the judge then gave no verdict (the cost cap stopped the call, the provider failed, or the reply could not be read), the citation carried `resolve_status: "ok"` and the judge's error under `resolve_error`, a field that says the source failed when it had not. A `resolve_error.kind` of `timeout` could have been either the fetch or the judge. Each citation now carries at most one of the two: `resolve_error` when the source was not resolved (`resolve_status` `skipped` or `error`), and `judge_error: { kind, message }` when it was and `judge` is absent. The kinds are unchanged: `cost_cap_reached`, `malformed_judge_response` and the provider kinds (`auth`, `rate_limit`, `bad_request`, `server_error`, `timeout`, `malformed_response`, `unknown`). Neither is scored as unsupported, and `IRIS_JUDGE_FAILED` still fires when every resolved citation fails at the judge. The stored evaluation's rule message now names what was not judged, by stage, for example `1/1 judged sources supported the output. Not judged: the judge failed on 1 resolved source (timeout); 1 source was not resolved (bad_status).`, which the dashboard shows on the evaluation. **A caller that read judge failures from `resolve_error` on a citation with `resolve_status: "ok"` reads them from `judge_error` instead.**

**`evaluate_output` is back to 0.19.0's speed, reading evaluations is faster than 0.19.0, and every number is unchanged (#717).** The risk estimate's 95% interval comes from 2,000 seeded draws. Since `answers_the_ask` advises instead of gating at the defaults, most evaluations reach the estimate, and on `main` it took about 8 ms of every call. It also ran on every read, because a stored evaluation re-composes its verdict when it is read: at 10,000 traces with 200 evaluated, `GET /api/v1/failures` took 2,946 ms on `main`, against 327 ms on 0.19.0. Three changes:
- Each draw rebuilt the failure classes with Maps and filters. Now the class structure is worked out once per estimate, and each draw is flat loops over the same values in the same order. The draws cannot be shared between detectors, because all of them come from one seeded stream.
- A finished estimate is cached (1,024 entries, least recently used evicted first), because it depends only on its detectors, prior and mode.
- The estimate is stored with each evaluation (migration 018, two columns and an index), under the key of the inputs it came from, and a read uses it only when the row's own inputs give the same key. Evaluations stored before the upgrade get theirs in the background after the start: on 20,000 evaluations written by 0.19.0, a tenth of them with a labelled fire of their own, the start took 138–183 ms, the fill took 14.8 s in steps of median 59 ms (the longest 140 ms), and a page of 50 read during it took 58–62 ms. Once every row is filled, a start reads nothing. Creating the index at the upgrade took 608 ms at 100,000 evaluations.
Measured with the same inputs, v0.19.0, `main` and this release alternated:
| | 0.19.0 | `main` | now |
|---|---|---|---|
| `evaluate_output` over stdio, median (300 calls × 3 rounds) | 3.1–3.7 ms | 11.3–13.9 ms | 3.2–3.9 ms |
| `evaluate_output`, p95 | 11.5–12.4 ms | 15.2–19.0 ms | 4.9–8.4 ms |
| `GET /api/v1/failures`, a fresh process, 10,000 traces with 200 evaluated | 319 ms | 2,971–3,006 ms | 131–134 ms |
| `GET /api/v1/moments`, the same | 106–109 ms | 790–795 ms | 80–83 ms |
| 500 evaluations read at once, each fire carrying a different label count | 4,452–4,484 ms | 4,462–4,498 ms | 107–113 ms |
HTTP ingest with `evaluate: true` goes from 25.7–26.8 ms on `main` to 14.6–15.4 ms, against 7.1–7.2 ms on 0.19.0. What remains is the agent failure-log query (#711), not the estimate.
`tests/unit/eval/risk-draws.test.ts` keeps the 0.19.0 loop and sampler as a reference. It requires every one of the 2,000 draws to match bit for bit over 800 generated inputs (fired and silent classes, local labels, duplicate rule names, both prior modes, and priors equal to three decimals), and the finished estimate to match whether it was cached or not. `tests/unit/storage/migration-016.test.ts` requires the verdict read back to equal composing the row again. It plants numbers under a row's own key to show a read uses the stored estimate, and shows that a stored estimate under another key, or one that is not an estimate, is ignored. It also checks the background fill and the fill's query plans. Against `main`'s build, 10,000 generated inputs gave no difference, and the verdicts and interpretations of the 500 labelled evaluations hash the same. `npm run proof -- --check --composite` regenerates the composite corpus's results unchanged.

**The dashboard sends compressed files and API responses (#718).** The dashboard build writes a brotli (`.br`) and a gzip (`.gz`) copy of each file it emits, at the strongest settings. The server sends the copy the browser accepts, with `Vary: Accept-Encoding`, and never serves a copy older than its file. JSON answers of 1 KB or more to a read (`GET` or `HEAD`) from another machine are compressed per request (brotli quality 4 or gzip level 6, off the event loop). The answer to a write is sent as it is: it is an acknowledgement, and compressing it only kept the writer waiting. On the same 10,000-trace store, HTTP ingest with `evaluate: true` took a median 9.0–13.9 ms with this rule and 10.7–15.6 ms when its 201 was compressed, 1.7 ms less in each of three paired rounds, while every read kept the sizes below. Measured on a 10,000-trace store:
| response | before | brotli | gzip only |
|---|---|---|---|
| first load of the dashboard | 363,007 bytes | 95,652 bytes | 110,169 bytes |
| a page of 50 traces | 59,523 bytes | 18,791 bytes | |
| a search page of 50 traces | 79,239 bytes | 20,338 bytes | |
| `/api/v1/capabilities` | 62,640 bytes | 20,124 bytes | |
A browser on plain `http://` to a LAN address offers gzip only. A client on the same machine (a loopback address) gets API answers uncompressed: there is no network to save, and compressing and decoding a page of 50 traces took `GET /api/v1/traces?limit=50` from 6.3 to 8.5 ms at 100,000 traces (#761). A reverse proxy on the same host connects over loopback too, and compresses for its own clients. The dashboard's files stay compressed on loopback, since they cost no CPU to send. Streamed responses (`res.write`, server-sent events) and non-JSON bodies pass through unchanged, as do responses that are marked `Cache-Control: no-transform` or already encoded. A browser request from another site (`Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` or `same-site`) is never compressed. This guards against BREACH: with compression, an attacker who can make a signed-in browser send requests carrying text of their choosing can read a secret in the same response from the response's length. The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`, so the only cross-site requests that carry it are top-level navigations, and browsers mark those as cross-site. The compressed copies add 389 KB to the npm package. Proved by `tests/unit/dashboard/compression.test.ts`, which reads the bytes on the wire and decodes them, and by `tests/e2e/compression.spec.ts`, where Chromium and Firefox load the built dashboard compressed.

**The public claims schema** (`iris-eval.com/claims-schema-v1.json`) requires `sdkPackage` in `version` and in `version.published` (the version of `@iris-eval/sdk`, and `false` until it is on npm), and now describes the top-level `clients` block `.claims.json` already carried, so the published file validates against its own schema again; a test holds the two together.

sections.title: Fixed
items: **`evaluate_output` with an `expected_trajectory` no longer fails with `IRIS_INTERNAL_ERROR`.** On the default bundle, and on `completeness` and `cost`, the response failed the tool's own output schema, which did not list `expected_trajectory` among the inputs a rule reads (`rule_results[].saw`). The schema now names every input, and a test holds it to the engine's list.

**A comparison no longer counts a rule that did not run as a pass.** A run row held only the rules that fired, so a rule that skipped on a case read the same as one that passed it. A second run that stopped sending its tool calls had every trajectory rule skip, passed every case, and `compare_runs` answered `better: true` with "This is an improvement" (reproduced end to end: 5 of 12 against 12 of 12, one-sided p 0.0078). Each rule is now compared only over the cases it ran on, and over the shared cases it ran on in both runs when they pair; a rule that ran in one run and on no case in the other has no difference and no test. `coverage.lost` names the rules that ran on fewer cases in the second run, the summary says so before it gives the rates, each case that "recovered" names the rules that did not run on it, and `better` is not declared while any coverage was lost. A regression is declared either way.

**A comparison's words match its numbers.** "This is a regression" could sit beside "95% interval [-28.6, +0.9]" and `significant: false`: the test was one-sided at 5% and the interval printed was the two-sided 95% one (45 of 50 against 38 of 50). The interval is now the 90% one that test reads, and the one-sided p is that interval inverted, so the word, the field and the interval agree on every input; a test checks every pair of rates at four run sizes, paired and unpaired. When the runs pair, the summary gives the share of changed cases that fell, with its exact interval, which is what McNemar's test reads.

**A comparison no longer calls runs "equivalent" within a margin nobody chose.** With no `equivalence_margin`, the margin defaulted to the smallest difference the run sizes could detect, so two runs of eight cases, both 8 of 8, read "Equivalent within 40.3 points", and a rise from 1 to 5 leaked-data failures in 12 cases read "Equivalent within 26.3 points". Equivalence is now tested only against a margin the caller supplies, on an interval over every case rather than only the changed ones, and never while a critical rule fires on new cases or coverage was lost.

**A critical rule firing on new cases is named in the comparison.** `critical_rises` lists each critical rule that fires on more cases in the second run, with the shared cases where it is new, and the summary states the count. The per-rule significance test could read "none reads worse" on five new leaks in twelve cases; the count is now given whatever the test says.

**`compare_traces` no longer prints a 95% interval of [100%, 100%].** The run-level interval was a percentile bootstrap over cases. Resampling cases that all passed returns the same answer every time, so the interval had no width whenever every case passed, and at 10 cases with a true pass rate of 95% it held the true rate two times in five (a seeded simulation of 2,000 trials). It is now the exact interval for that many cases, each case counted once at its own rate, which holds the true rate at least 93 times in 100 at 10, 20 and 50 cases for rates from 50% to 99%.

**"Could not have detected a change smaller than X" now means what it says.** X was the half-width of the 95% interval at a pass rate of one half, which is the difference a test detects about half the time. It is now the difference detected four times in five (80% power), for the one-sided test a run comparison makes and the two-sided one the dashboard's drift view makes, and the sentence says "would have missed, more often than one time in five".

**The dashboard no longer draws a rule that never ran as "100% pass".** The Drift page's per-rule meters counted a rule as passing on every trace where it was not in the failed list, so a rule that skipped on all 84 evaluations of a run showed a full bar titled "84 firings, 100% pass", and the header counted 84 × 25 "rule firings". A meter's rate is now over the traces the rule ran on; a rule that ran on none reads "not run (84)" with an empty bar; the header counts the checks that ran and says how many did not. The moments API carries `ruleSnapshot.passed`, the rules that ran and passed, beside `failed` and `skipped`.

**The run comparison page shows what each run was judged on.** It lists the rules that ran on fewer cases in the second run and the critical rules firing on new cases, shows each rule's failures as "3 of 20" (the cases it ran on) or "not run", and marks a comparison where more cases passed under fewer checks as "JUDGED ON LESS" instead of "BETTER". The summary rendered literal `**` markers; it is plain text now.

**Several server processes on one Iris home run the same rules and lose no rule.** `install` gives each MCP client its own server process, and they share `custom-rules.json`. Each process read the file once at start and wrote its own copy back on every change. A rule deployed through one client was not applied by the others, two processes stamped different `ruleset_hash` values on the same output at the same moment, and the next deploy from a process that started earlier deleted every rule deployed since. A process now checks the file before an evaluation (one `stat`, no read, at most once every 20 ms) and re-reads it when it changed, and a change is made under a lock file on what the file holds at that moment. `rules_changed` counts a change another process made. A rules file that could not be parsed is read again once it is fixed, without a restart. A test starts two servers on one home and holds each of these; another has three processes deploy at once and counts the rules afterwards.

**A label written through one server process is read by the others.** Labels are in the database, which the processes share, but each read them once at start, so a label moved the local precision and the prior only in the process it was written through. Each process now reads the database's change counter before an evaluation (at most once every 20 ms) and re-reads the labels when another process wrote one.

**The retention sweep no longer deletes the pinned baseline run.** A baseline is the run every later run is compared against, and the sweep deleted it at `retention.days` like any other trace: a run pinned 31 days earlier compared against nothing. Its traces and evaluations are now kept until the run is unpinned, and each sweep that keeps some of it says so in the log. `delete_trace` and `--purge` remove them as before. Dataset cases and labels were never swept; a test now holds that.

**The HTTP endpoint serves more than one MCP client.** `--transport http` created one transport for the life of the process. The first client to `initialize` owned it, a second got `400 Server already initialized`, and after the first ended its session every later client got `404 Session not found` until the server was restarted. Each `initialize` now opens a session of its own over the one engine and store, up to 256 at a time. Clients often leave without `DELETE /mcp`, so at the limit a new client takes the place of the session used least recently when that session has no event stream open and has been quiet for a minute; when every session is in use the new client gets `503` with `Retry-After`. Shutdown ends the open sessions first, so an open event stream no longer holds it for ten seconds.

**The site and the docs say what the code does, and a test holds each of these statements to the thing it describes.**
- What leaves the machine. The sentence the README, the site, `llms.txt` and the MCP manifest print (`brand.dataResidency`) names all four ways out, each off until you configure it: the OpenTelemetry exporter, the LLM judge, the citation check that fetches the pages an output cites (`verify_citations`), and webhooks. It named the first two, and the security page, which now prints the sentence, said "No data ever leaves your environment". `tests/data-residency-names-every-exit.test.ts` lists every source file that opens an outbound connection with the words the sentence must carry for it, so a fifth way out fails until it is named.
- Which checks block a merge. The list is `.github/required-checks.json`: a test holds `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/proof.md` to it, and a new job in the claims workflow compares it with the live branch protection on every pull request and push. The proof job is a required check, so a rule change cannot merge without its numbers, as `docs/proof.md` says. `CONTRIBUTING.md` had typed a shorter list and a Prettier check CI does not run.
- The proof corpus. `docs/proof.md` and `proof/README.md` describe the blind sample as twenty cases from each of seven families (they called it "40-case"); say the real transcripts are measured on their own, every transcript-derived case having left the families on 2026-09-23; name the judgement families no human has sampled, where they said every rule outside the sample is arithmetic; and describe the risk composer as what the server composes every verdict with, where they called it "run in the harness only" and something "a future release may adopt". `tests/proof/proof-docs-match-corpus.test.ts` checks each against the corpus headers, the sample manifest and the tree.
- The capability map. `compare_traces` has taken `question` since 0.15.0, so four multi-run cells are answered (`has`) on the same evidence the completion row already cited, and two keep a limit that still holds; all six had said "a per-question filter is not shipped". No cell says `GET /api/v1/cases/:key` takes the filter, which it does not. Three more cells agree with the rows beside them: recall by entity and recall under evasion transforms, which those rows publish, and which rule reads the structure of the ask (`ask_coverage`). The contract test reads the tool's schema and the route's.
- The site. The live playground says beside the box that the text is posted to the site's server, and what is kept: a salted hash of the address for the rate limit, the category, a length bucket, the result and the duration, never the text. Its description had said the rules run "in your browser". The Cursor button installs Iris under the key `iris-eval`, as every other surface does, in place of `server`. Every homepage card metric reads from the truthbase, with its unit; "60s to first trace" and "$0.07 avg cost visibility per trace", which nothing measured, are replaced. The Output Quality Score page says the composer never consults the score for `passed` and that `/proof` publishes the verdict's numbers, where it said `passed` is "decided by the threshold" and that how the composed verdict performs "is not yet measured".

**The compare pages hold against the vendors' pages as of 2026-10-01.** Every statement about the fourteen vendors was read again against their own docs, pricing and changelogs, not only the quoted sentence, and the cells that had stopped being true were corrected: Phoenix runs LLM-as-a-judge and code evaluators server-side, and its MCP server is the remote one built into Phoenix 19 and later; Langfuse and DeepEval score with Jev as a judge, and Confident AI offers it; Langfuse's MCP server has read and write tools on Cloud and self-hosted; Promptfoo's trajectory assertions read OpenTelemetry spans the app sends; LangSmith's standalone MCP server is deprecated for its hosted Remote MCP, and LangSmith and Weave accept OpenTelemetry spans; Weights & Biases is part of CoreWeave Forge; Patronus AI documents SDK prompt management, and the MCP server repository its blog links returned 404; Opik lists 30+ pre-built metrics, LLM-as-a-judge and heuristic; Latitude has no prompt manager in V2 and lists its ISO 27001 audit and GDPR review as in progress; Judgment's $32M covers its Seed and Series A; Helicone's AI Gateway repository is GPL-3.0. `npm run compare:verify` finds all 179 quoted sentences on their pages, and the dates on the pages say 2026-10-01.

**Closing the store releases the file before it returns (#750).** The checkpoint worker's connection was asked to close and given 5 s; past that the thread was terminated and `close()` returned at once, while the thread was still in its statement and still held `iris.db` open. On Windows the file could not then be moved or removed until that statement ended, and two storage suites failed on `windows-latest` removing their directories (`EPERM`) after every assertion had passed. `close()` now resolves only once the thread has ended, and answers any request the thread was in with an error rather than leaving it waiting. A test holds the worker in a four-second statement with a 100 ms timeout: before the change `close()` returned with the thread still running (4 runs in 4, both drivers); now it waits for it.
- The checkpoint thread stays held from the start of `close()` until it has ended. The answer to a checkpoint in flight used to release it again. If the thread then outlasted `close()`'s timeout, a short-lived process (`iris-eval ingest`, say) could exit with code 13 while `close()` still waited. The worker-exit CI job showed that release when ending the thread directly, in 1 process in 10.

**A search's page of trace ids, and the start's check for evaluations with no stored risk estimate, keep their plans when the file has statistics (#742).** Iris never writes statistics, but `ANALYZE` run by hand does, and under them SQLite read the search index's whole trace_id index to find a page's ids, and every evaluation to find the ones without a risk estimate, at every start. The page's ids are now looked up one doc id at a time in a fixed join, in one statement for any number of matches (100,000 in 80 ms at 100,000 traces, against 92 ms in chunks of 1,000), and the fill names its index. The query-plan test covers every export read, and `getEvalsByTraceIds` names the index it already used.

**The website builds only when something its build reads has changed.** Every pull request used to create a preview build of iris-eval.com, and one day of pull requests used up the host's daily build allowance, which the live site's production deploys share. A preview now builds only for a change to `website/` or `docs/blog/`, and a production deploy also for a `.claims.json` change other than its timestamp and commit stamp. A branch's first deployment compares with `main`, and a base the host's shallow clone lacks is fetched; anything that fails builds. `tests/website-build-scope.test.ts` runs the real skip script in a shallow clone, as the host does, for six kinds of change, a branch's first deployment and an unreachable base, and fails if a website source reads any other path in the repository. CI's website job now runs the production build (`next build`) on every pull request, so a `.claims.json` change that would break the site is still caught without a preview.

**A database file is never opened by both copies of SQLite in one process (#739).** better-sqlite3 carries its own SQLite and `node:sqlite` is Node's. Their locks cannot see each other within one process, and one can reset the WAL's shared-memory file while the other has it mapped, which kills the process with SIGBUS or corrupts the file. Measured on Linux with Node 24.21.0: SIGBUS in 3 runs of 5, against 0 of 10 with one copy. Iris never did this: the store and its two worker threads use the copy the store's connection got. The one place it happened was a test's stand-in search thread, which died of SIGBUS in 2 of 30 runs on macOS. Now the driver seam enforces it: a file already open in a thread is opened again only with the copy that holds it, and the other copy is refused before it opens anything. A new CI job ends worker threads that hold a connection every way Iris ends them, on Linux, macOS and Windows, Node 22 and 24, both drivers: 9,000 per cell. One process in one cell has since exited with an access violation, on Windows with Node 24. That is a Node.js bug in a thread's teardown (nodejs/node#65778), which the job reached by starting its threads with tsx's loader; an installed server's threads have none (#804). A cell takes 20 to 60 minutes, so the job runs on pull requests that touch storage, its fixtures or the dependencies, on every push to `main`, and nightly.

**Scoring a trace no longer reads every evaluation in the store (#711).** Each evaluation with a cost reads its agent's recent history (the failure log), and so do `/api/v1/moments`, `/api/v1/failures`, the views and webhook moment events. There are two ways to read that history, and which one is fast depends on the data. 0.19.0 always read every evaluation of the store; the covering index added for search moved SQLite to walking every trace instead; with statistics it picked the slow way for a store where every trace is evaluated. The read now chooses between two queries that name their index and fix their join order, using counts of index entries. At 100,000 traces with every trace evaluated, `log_trace` with `evaluate: true` took 291 ms in 0.19.0 and takes 25.7 ms, `POST /api/v1/traces` with evaluate 291 ms and 24.9 ms, and `GET /api/v1/moments` 2.1 s and 0.8 s (medians of three rounds). The failure-log read itself went from 160 to 176 ms to 3 ms. On a store with few evaluations, where 0.19.0 was already fast, it stays between 0.1 and 3.5 ms. A test checks every result against the plain query on 12 seeded random stores per driver, through all three of the read's paths.

**Every hot read keeps its query plan, whatever SQLite's statistics say (#711).** Iris never runs `ANALYZE`. With statistics from a store of 100,000 evaluated traces, SQLite made the failure log 35 times slower and the 30-day summary 2.4 times slower. The reads that run on every evaluation or dashboard render (the failure log, case results, `get_traces` with and without `q`, the trace search join, the filter lists, the summary and the eval stats) now name their index and fix their join order. `tests/unit/storage/query-plans.test.ts` checks each statement's plan on both drivers, with and without FTS5, with no statistics and under three sets of them. The test fails if a statement reads a whole table, or if a join starts from the wrong side or reaches the other side through the wrong index.

**The dashboard's first render reads index entries, not trace rows (#711).** At 100,000 traces: `GET /api/v1/filters` 198 ms in 0.19.0, 1.4 ms now (one index seek per distinct agent and framework); `GET /api/v1/summary?hours=720` 284 ms and 62 ms; `GET /api/v1/eval-stats?period=30d` 172 ms and 33 ms. `get_traces` sorted by `cost_usd` or `latency_ms` sorts index entries and reads the 50 rows of the page: 187 ms and 27 ms.

**`get_traces` with `min_score` or `max_score` no longer walks every evaluation once per trace (#711).** Finding each trace's latest evaluation took the tenant's evaluations in time order instead of the trace's own one or two. At 100,000 evaluated traces the count for one page ran for more than two minutes; the page and its count take 0.2 s now. 0.19.0 had the same plan.

**Case results for one case key or one session start from that case's traces (#711).** A webhook reads them for each evaluation. At 100,000 evaluated traces the read took 290 ms and takes under 0.1 ms. 0.19.0 had the same plan.

**On Node's built-in `node:sqlite`, the first read after another process changed the schema returns every column (#711).** `node:sqlite` counts a statement's columns before SQLite recompiles it for the new schema. That first read dropped a column that had just been added, and failed on a table rebuilt with fewer columns. This happened even to a statement prepared fresh. A read now checks the schema version first and has the connection load the new schema when it moved.

**Rebuilding the search index no longer holds the server while the old index is erased (#695).** When the index has to be rebuilt from scratch (a file opened by a SQLite without FTS5, then by one with it), the old index used to be dropped in one statement, which rewrites and zeroes every page of it: at 100,000 agent-loop traces the event loop was held for 3.1 s in both of two runs over stdio (5.2 s in the issue, and up to 19.7 s in one run of the adapter alone). The old index is now erased a few hundred rows at a time before the rebuild indexes anything, each freed page zeroed as before, and the emptied tables are then dropped. Over stdio at 100,000 the longest hold during the erasure and the rebuild was 247 ms and 211 ms; at 10,000, 90 to 236 ms against 336 ms to 3.1 s. FTS5's own tables are read-only to SQL on a connection in SQLite's defensive mode, which better-sqlite3 turns on, so each step turns it off for its own statements and back on; a connection that refuses the write anyway drops the old index in one statement, as before, and logs a warning that says so.

**A write no longer waits for SQLite to copy the whole write-ahead log into the database file, and the log stays short.** SQLite does that copy (a checkpoint) inside whichever commit takes the log past 1,000 pages, and on a large file that commit was the slow one: at 100,000 agent-loop traces, sweep steps that committed in 3 ms at the median took up to 567 ms when a checkpoint landed in them, and with the automatic checkpoint switched off the slowest of them took 20 ms (60 steps, two runs each). A worker thread with its own connection to the file now copies the log, 250 ms after each copy ends. A copy on another connection cannot start the log over while writes keep coming, so the server's own connection still checkpoints, at 16,000 pages (64 MB) instead of 1,000, and copies only what the worker has not. Before each step of background work, once the log holds 8,000 pages, the worker empties it and the step waits for that without holding the event loop. The worker also empties the log when a delete, a sweep or `--purge` asks. When the worker's own work holds that off (its connection still opening after the store's first write, or a copy in progress), the delete waits for the worker and has it empty the log, trying again for up to 250 ms with the event loop free, so the text is gone when the call returns. Every write of the server's own also waits for a TRUNCATE in flight, off the event loop, as the background steps already did: the TRUNCATE takes the write lock without waiting, and a write that landed in that instant turned it away, so under steady writes a delete could return with its text still in the file (with Node's built-in SQLite, in 2 runs of 3 of 20 deletes while another client wrote). A test now deletes 20 traces while another client writes on every turn of the event loop, and checks the file's bytes after each one. Only a search, or another process using the file, still leaves the erasure to the retry every 20 ms. Before, the worker opening was treated like a reader, and on a Windows runner with Node's built-in SQLite a deleted trace's words were still in `iris.db` when `delete_trace` returned. A stress test deletes 96 traces across 12 stores, each while the index is built, the worker copies and, for the first delete of each store, the worker is still starting, and checks the file's bytes after every call. It also found `delete_trace` failing with "database is locked" when a worker TRUNCATE landed between its read and its write (3 times in 26 runs): the delete now takes the write lock before it reads, after any TRUNCATE in flight. Until the worker is running, and if it ever stops, the server's own connection checkpoints as before, and a warning says so. A database in memory has no worker. Measured at 100,000 agent-loop traces against the worker alone, which let the log grow with every write:
- 1,000 `log_trace` calls over stdio, three runs: 1.05 to 1.26 ms at the median instead of 1.28 to 1.46 ms, the slowest 1% 22 to 25 ms instead of 25 to 27 ms, and a 63 to 65 MB log instead of 153 MB. With the worker alone, every read and write on the server's connection looked through the whole log. 0.19.0 takes 0.67 to 0.77 ms; what is left of the difference is the search index's own write (the entry on the statement cache has it).
- The search index built after an upgrade from 0.19.0, in one process, two runs: a 10 to 22 MB log at the end instead of 2.6 GB, the longest hold of the event loop 62 to 72 ms instead of 193 to 195 ms, and 66 to 69 s instead of 64 s.
- How far the log runs past 64 MB before it starts over depends on the disk. The tail checkpoint waits while the worker's own copy holds the checkpoint lock, and SQLite reuses the log file without shrinking it, so the file keeps its largest cycle. Under 6,000 back-to-back writes at 10,000 traces the log started over about every 500 to 600 ms both on a desktop, where the file reached 63 to 67 MB, and on a hosted Linux runner, where cycles reached 105 to 138 MB. With the worker alone it started over twice and reached 1.1 GB. The stall guard asserts the restarts (the longest stretch over 64 MB without one stays under 2 s) and a 256 MB ceiling.

**A failing test in the truthbase capture is reported as a failing test, by name, not as drift.** On `main` at 969719e the CI truthbase job said only "claims.json drifted from generator output". The tree was byte-identical to a pull-request head whose same job had passed; one test had failed during the capture (3,729 of 3,730), was recorded as `failed: 1`, and no line of the log named it. The capture now refuses a run with a failing test and lists each one with its file and the first line of its failure, and `claims:check` names every field that differs from the generator's output (for that run it would have printed `tests.vitestRoot.passed: committed 3730, generated 3729`).

**The truthbase capture refuses a run that exited non-zero with every test passing.** An unhandled error leaves vitest's JSON report at `success: true` with every test passed; only the exit code says the run failed, and the report and its output do not carry the error. So the capture's rule for a run that failed outside any test (it read `success: false`) never fired, and a branch recorded 4,016 of 4,016 while CI failed its test jobs on an unhandled rejection. The capture now reads the exit code and refuses such a run, saying to run `npx vitest run` in the scope to see the error. A scope that wrote no report is unchanged: it keeps the committed counts, which the CI job that cannot install the dashboard relies on.

**The Python client's publish workflow parses again, and every workflow is linted on every pull request.** Since the hash-pinned build landed, `publish-python.yml` held a plain YAML value with `:all: -r` in it, which YAML reads as a mapping, so GitHub refused the file on every push. Nothing noticed, because the workflow ran only on a `py-v*` tag. The step is now a block scalar. A new CI job runs actionlint 1.7.12, from an image pinned by digest, over every workflow in `.github/workflows`, including each `run:` script through shellcheck. It reported the parse error on the old file, and 6 shellcheck findings elsewhere, now fixed (four unguarded `ls *.tgz` globs in `ci.yml`, an unused loop variable and an unquoted `kill $(cat …)` in `lighthouse.yml`). `publish-python.yml` now also runs its build job on every pull request (the hashed install, the build and the fresh-environment import), and publishes only for a tag.

**`o1-mini` is priced at $1.10 in and $4.40 out per million tokens, not $3 and $12.** The judge's table carried the model's launch price; OpenAI's model page (developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/o1-mini) lists $1.10 / $4.40, and its pricing page no longer lists the model. The judge's cost cap and cost report for `o1-mini` were 2.7 times too high, so the cap refused calls that fit. Every other row was checked against claude.com/pricing and developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing on 2026-09-28 and matches, and the table's read date is now 2026-09-28.

**On Node 24, Iris no longer loads a better-sqlite3 that would abort the server when it frees a statement (#719).** Node 24.19.0 changed the `node::ObjectWrap` header without the runtime change it needs ([nodejs/node#65446](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/65446)). A better-sqlite3 compiled against that header, as npm does when the prebuilt download fails, aborts the process with `Assertion failed: (env) != nullptr` the first time V8 collects one of its statements, whether the database is open or closed. On Node 24.21.0 with 12.11.1, measured: a binary built from source aborted in 10 runs of 10, the prebuilt binary in 0 of 10. It aborted CI once, in 1 of the 62 failed jobs of the last 400 runs, the one whose install had compiled the addon. Iris now reads the binary before loading it. When the binary carries the new call and the runtime lacks the fix (every 24.x release so far, and 26.x before 26.4.0), Iris holds the store with Node's built-in SQLite and says why on stderr and in `--self-test`; `GET /health` reports `driver: "node"`. `IRIS_SQLITE_DRIVER=native` refuses instead. `npm rebuild better-sqlite3` restores the prebuilt binary, which is safe. A new CI job compiles the addon from source on Node 24 on Linux, macOS and Windows, and on Node 22 on Linux and macOS. It requires the binary to abort under collection exactly when Iris predicts it, and a real server started and stopped over stdio six times to end every session cleanly. With the check turned off, that stdio test failed 5 runs of 5 on the compiled binary.

**A stdio server shuts down in order when the client closes its stdin.** MCP clients end a stdio session that way. The server used to drain and exit without closing the store, and a search-index build kept running for the client that had gone: 1.5 s on 80,000 traces, against 32 ms now. With the dashboard running, the end of stdin still does not stop the process.

**A published precision's interval is the one for the prevalence asked (#717).** The intervals behind a rule's positive predictive value and miss rate were remembered per rule and prevalence to three decimals, but computed at the exact prevalence. So the first prevalence asked answered for every other that rounded the same: after an interval at 0.0101, one at 0.0104 came back as 0.0101's. An estimated prior is a continuous number, so a deployment with labels could see an interval for another prior. The intervals are now remembered per exact prevalence (4,096 entries, least recently used evicted first). The posterior draws, which depend on the rule alone, are drawn once per rule. `tests/unit/eval/accuracy.test.ts` fails on the old key, and it checks every rule at eight prevalences against intervals drawn afresh as before.

**`--self-test` no longer says PASS on a database the server then refuses (#704).** It checked that the configured home was writable and ran everything else in a temporary home, so a file migrated by a newer release, or MCP clients pinned to a release that could no longer open it, passed. Two new steps read the configured database on a read-only connection and each MCP client's config: the first fails when this version cannot open the file, naming the version it needs, `install --upgrade` and the newest copy to restore, and otherwise says what the next start will apply; the second fails when a client is pinned to a release that cannot open the file, and warns when the next start will strand one. Neither changes the file: the tests compare its SHA-256 before and after.

**A trace stored by a process that does not index it is found by the next search.** A trace inserted by hand, or by a release from before the search index, had no entry in the index, and a server already running answered searches from the index without it until its next start. Before each search the server now looks for traces added since the last one that the index lacks (a lookup of the newest row id, then of each new row in the index's own id table); if it finds any, that search reads the traces and the index takes them in behind it.

**A start refused over the database prints its sentence on its own line.** The refusal reached the terminal only inside a structured log record with a stack trace; the sentence is now written plain to stderr first, as `iris-eval: This database was migrated by a newer Iris …`.

**Every test file is type-checked in CI (#721).** `tsconfig.json` covers `src/` only, so no file under `tests/` was ever type-checked. On main, a config that includes `tests/` and resolves modules the way Vitest does found 95 errors across the test files and 1 in the Playwright setup.
- 53 errors cast `client.callTool`'s result union to `{ content?: unknown }`, and 4 read a resource's `text` without checking it was not a blob. Shared helpers in `tests/helpers/` now narrow both and throw naming what arrived.
- Three fixtures had drifted from the types: a `count` evidence item used `name` where the type has `stat` and `unit`, an e2e rule result said it saw `cost_usd` (a rule needs `cost`), and failure-log entries lacked `costUsd`.
- Test files added since found 12 more: an export test's untyped id list and query objects, two more resource reads not checked for a blob (now `resourceTextOf`), an upgrade test reading `cost_source` off `resolveTraceCost`'s inferred literal type, and `checkReport`'s `exitCode` option, which the script's own types did not name (it now has a JSDoc signature).
- `npm run typecheck:tests` checks `tests/` under `tsconfig.tests.json`, and the Playwright specs under `tsconfig.e2e.json` with the DOM library, since their page callbacks run in the browser. The new CI job `typecheck-tests` runs it. The dashboard's tests were already checked by its own typecheck.

**The published test counts are no longer recorded from a run in which a test file failed to load.** `npm run claims:capture-tests` read only vitest's totals, and a file that does not parse or throws at import counts none of its tests and no failure, so a run eleven tests short once recorded every test passing. The capture now refuses such a run, naming each file and the first line of its error, and writes nothing; it also refuses a run vitest marks failed with no failing test, and a run with a skipped test (which it used to fall back from to the committed counts). `--report root=<file>` and `--report dashboard=<file>` read an existing vitest JSON report instead of running the suite, which is how `tests/unit/scripts/capture-report.test.ts` proves the refusal on a real report of a file that fails to parse and one that throws at import.

**The Python recorder batches as it says it does.** `IrisRecorder` waits `flush_interval` (0.25 s by default) to gather traces into one request, but every new trace woke that wait early, so an application recording steadily sent one request per trace and a full queue was never reached. The interval is now a deadline that only `flush()` or `close()` ends early. `test_the_queue_is_bounded_and_drops_the_oldest` yields between records, and fails on the old recorder every run.

**The Failures and Moments pages no longer re-run the regression-alarm watcher once per trace (#680).** To find the alarms each trace in its window carries, the route re-ran every rule's CUSUM watcher over the agent's log up to that trace, so the cost grew with the square of the window and with the number of rules. The watchers now run once per request, and once more for each size of the rule family the log grows through; a log whose rules and runs are there from the start takes one pass. Every trace gets exactly the alarms it got before: a test checks the one pass against the per-trace answer for every trace of seeded logs where rules and runs start part-way through, where traces share a timestamp, and where alarms fire. On one agent's 500 traces the Failures and ranked Moments responses are byte-identical before and after. Measured on that window with no other load: with 25 rules, a warm request takes 286–344 ms, down from 2.5–2.6 s, and the first request after a start 4.5 s, down from 6.8 s; with 3 rules, 33–45 ms, down from 94–101 ms. The first-request cost that remains is the simulation that draws each stream's alarm line, which is memoised once drawn.

**The first Failures or Moments request after a start no longer spends seconds drawing alarm lines.** Each stream's regression-alarm line came from a seeded simulation of about 150 ms, run the first time the stream's baseline settled, so a server's first request with 25 rules spent most of its time simulating. The lines are now generated ahead of time into `src/eval/cusum-thresholds.generated.ts`: every baseline a stream can first settle at, 2,267 of them up to 2,000 evaluations, which covers a rule whose tenth fail comes at a fail rate down to about 0.5%. A stream that settles later than that is simulated on first use, as before. Each row is exactly what the simulation returns, and a CI job, `npm run cusum:check`, regenerates every row from its seed and fails when the committed table differs. On one agent's 500 traces the Failures, ranked Moments and newest-first Moments responses are identical before and after, apart from the rank scores, which decay with the clock. Measured on that window with no other load, three runs each: with 25 rules the first request takes 188–216 ms, down from 4.5–4.9 s; with 3 rules, 98–103 ms, down from 497–541 ms.

**A busy host no longer gets ordinary custom regex rules killed as backtracking (#677).** The regex sandbox's 100 ms budget ran from the moment a match was posted, so the time the worker thread waited to be scheduled was charged to the pattern. With every core busy, a pattern as plain as `forbidden` on a 40-character output was killed and reported as a budget skip, and a critical rule came back in `critical_skipped` with the verdict unknown, exactly when the server was busiest. Two changes fix it. The budget now starts when the worker starts the match. A fresh worker also warms the match path before it reports ready, so its first match does not pay inside the budget for code the thread has not run yet. A worker that has not started a match within 5 s is reported as a sandbox error, never as backtracking. A catastrophic pattern is still killed one budget after it starts. Under 20 busy-loop processes on a 20-core machine, the root test suite failed `critical-rule-budget-killed` in 2 of 5 runs and `rules-preview`'s sample check in 1 of 5 before, and neither in 10 runs after. A harness with 60 busy processes (`scripts/sandbox-load-harness.ts`) ran 7,600 matches of `forbidden` with no false timeout, against 2 in 1,000 before. `^(a|a)*$` on 41 characters was still killed every time.

**LangGraph traces from LangSmith's OpenTelemetry export arrive readable.** LangSmith sends `gen_ai.prompt` / `gen_ai.completion` as bytes, which OTLP/JSON writes as base64, so the trace's input and output were stored as base64. Bytes that hold UTF-8 text are now read as that text, and a LangChain envelope (a run's whole state as `{"messages": [...]}`, or a model's `{"generations": ...}`) is read down to the last question asked and the last answer given. Proven by a captured export of a real LangGraph run (`tests/fixtures/otlp/langsmith-langgraph.pb`) and by CI running the recipe against a real server.

**A tool call whose arguments arrive as a JSON string is checked as the object it encodes.** `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` (and `tool_call.function.arguments`, `ai.toolCall.args`) are JSON strings by convention, and the OpenTelemetry Python SDK can send no other form; `valid_tool_arguments` read the string and failed every such call against its tool's schema, which turned a correct tool loop into a `fail` verdict.

**The LangGraph recipe works as written.** LangSmith posts to `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` without appending `/v1/traces` and does not percent-decode `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`; the recipe's endpoint and header lines now say so, and `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` names the agent.

**The LangChain and CrewAI examples are complete programs, not scaffolds.** `examples/langchain/observe-agent.py` is a LangGraph agent with `IrisCallbackHandler` (CI runs the same graph with a scripted model); `examples/crewai/observe-crew.py` is the CrewAI OpenInference recipe as a script. Each needs a model key to run.

**The published list of judge models is the list the judge accepts.** `llmJudgeTemplates.supportedModels` in `.claims.json` was typed by hand. It named `o1-mini`, which the judge marks retired, and no Claude 5 model. It is now read from the pricing table the judge enforces, and a test holds the two equal.

**`answers_the_ask` has blocked at the shipped defaults since 0.18.0, contrary to its release notes; it now advises there, as documented.** The 0.18.0 notes said it advises unless you set a relevance threshold. On every server built from its config it blocked. Its two measurements decided whether a threshold was yours by comparing the value with the number in the rule's own file, and the shipped config carries `topic_consistency: 0.33` where the rule says 1/3, so the shipped default read as your setting. The unit tests built engines without the shipped config, so none of them saw it. `keyword_overlap`, `topic_consistency`, `min_output_length`, `sentence_count` and `tool_choice` now read where a threshold came from — your config file, or the context a caller passes — never its value, like every other rule. A deployment that sets the shipped number has still set it. `tests/unit/eval/shipped-thresholds-read-as-shipped.test.ts` builds the engine from `loadConfig()` and `defaultConfig` and requires every threshold stamp to read `default` at the defaults; it fails on the old code.

**The published composite numbers move, because they were measured with the rule blocking.** The composite corpus runs the shipped config, so `answers_the_ask` was blocking in the measurement too, and failing stub and off-task cases that no other layer catches. At the shipped settings the risk composer is now right about shipping on 64.7% of the test split (95% interval 47.9–78.5%; was 76.5%) and 75.7% of dev (66.9–82.7%; was 81.1%). It now misses 45.8% of the outputs that should be blocked on test (was 29.2%) and 26.3% on dev (was 18.4%). False blocks on clean outputs do not change (10.0% on test, 20.0% on dev), nor do the real-transcript and per-class rows. Twelve composite verdicts change: five stub cases, four off-task cases and one stub-and-over-budget case now pass; two cases that also carry injection still fail, one on the risk estimate and one on a detector's veto. The per-output advantage over the legacy composer on test falls from 41.2 to 29.4 points (5.7–48.9). In the calibration table behind `verdict.confidence`, the 0.1–0.2 band holds 16 bad verdicts of 43 (was 12 of 39), and 69 of 112 labelled verdicts move from decisive to marginal (was 63 of 101). No rule's precision, recall or F1 moved.
**The response schema accepts a judge's `sample` evidence** and the rule result's `judge` object. Before, a response carrying either failed the output-schema check.

**The evaluator matrix reads a measured `proof/judge-results.json`.** It looked templates up by name in an array, so a keyed run would still have read as pending. It also derives the judge case count from the case files instead of the stale "165 cases across the five templates".

**A fresh clone builds with `pnpm install && pnpm run build` again.** Since the dashboard joined `build` in 0.13.0, a clone that installed only the root package had no dashboard dependencies, so the build stopped at `Cannot find package 'vite'`. Directories that build Iris from its repository, Glama among them, have failed to build it since, and kept showing 0.10.0 and nine tools. `build:dashboard` now installs the dashboard's dependencies from its lockfile when they are missing, and a CI job builds from a fresh checkout with pnpm and requires every tool in `tools/list`.

**`npm run demo` and the release and tool-list checks no longer start Iris on your own data.** `npm run demo` started the server on `~/.iris`, so its traces were stored in the database of the Iris you use and the checkout's migrations were applied to it; a database migrated by a newer checkout is then refused by the installed release. The demo, `scripts/check-tools-listed.mjs` and `npm run verify:release` now start it with `IRIS_HOME` and `IRIS_DB_PATH` both set to a temporary directory they remove, over any the caller has set. `tests/unit/scripts/check-tools-listed.test.ts` runs the check against a stand-in server that answers only when both are set, and requires the caller's own home to be left untouched. The test setup also clears an `IRIS_DB_PATH` exported in the caller's shell, so `npm test` keeps every database in its scratch home.

**The dashboard works from the keyboard and reads correctly to a screen reader, and CI now checks it on every page in both themes (#724).**
- The view tabs carry the ids their panels name (each panel pointed at a tab id that was not on the page), are one Tab stop, and move with Left, Right, Home and End. The period selector sits beside the tablist instead of inside it, which axe rated critical (`aria-required-children`). The Time period and Cohort radio groups are one Tab stop each and move with the arrow keys.
- Each sparkline on the Drift and Health views is named for its agent or rule; axe found 25 unnamed on the Drift view (`svg-img-alt`).
- The account menu and the notifications popover move focus into themselves when opened, give it back to their button on Escape, and close when focus leaves them. The menu's items move with Up and Down, and Down on its button opens it. The command palette and the keyboard-shortcuts overlay keep focus inside while open and give it back on close; opening the tour from the palette used to leave focus on the page body. The palette's input is a combobox that controls a named listbox, and the selected option scrolls into view as the arrows move it.
- The links on the not-found page are underlined, so they differ from the text around them by more than colour.
- The Export button on the Traces and Evaluations lists names its panel in `aria-controls` only while the panel is open; closed, it named an id that was not on the page.
- `tests/e2e/a11y.spec.ts` runs axe-core 4.12.1 (WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 at A and AA, and best practice) on every route: 17 addresses, counting each dashboard view and the not-found page, in the dark and light themes, and on the five overlays open. It checks that every id an ARIA attribute or a `<label>` names is on the page, walks each page with Tab to its end (no trap, a visible focus indicator on every stop, every stop on screen, every control reached or in a group whose Tab stop is), and fails if a route in `dashboard/src/routes.tsx` has no entry. It runs in Chromium and Firefox; against the dashboard before this change, 19 of its Chromium cases fail. Colour contrast is enforced too (next entry).

**Dashboard text reaches WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) in both themes (#725).** axe counted 934 text elements below it on the 17 addresses above, counting each page separately (432 in the dark theme, 502 in the light): the muted text at 2.86 to 3.38:1, and in the light theme the pass, warn and fail colours at 1.72 to 3.76:1. Each colour keeps its hue and moves only in lightness (in OKLCH), to the nearest value that reaches 4.5:1 on every surface and tint it is drawn on:
- `--text-muted`: dark `#5e5e72` to `#7d7e93`, light `#7a908e` to `#5a6f6e`.
- Light theme only: `--eval-pass` `#22c55e` to `#007532`, `--eval-warn` `#eab308` to `#886600`, `--eval-fail` `#ef4444` to `#c50b20`. In the dark theme `--eval-fail` goes from `#ef4444` to `#fc514f`, the same hue lifted in lightness, because as text on its own chip tint it measured 4.1 to 4.4:1 (the verdict panel's basis chip on a moment, and a delete in the audit log, in Firefox); it is now 4.7:1 or more on every dark surface and tint. The solid destructive button keeps `#ef4444` (`--danger-fill`). The dark theme's pass and warn colours already pass.
- `--eval-skipped` `#71717a`: dark `#8b8b94`, light `#6a6a73`.
- The red of the fail badges on their `#450a0a` fill: `#ef4444` to `#f44948`.
- Text on a teal fill (primary buttons, the notification count) is the near-black `--text-on-accent` in both themes. The light theme drew it in `#fafcfc` on `#14b8a6` (2.4:1), and `.iris-btn--primary` drew white on `#0d9488` (3.7:1), and on `#14b8a6` when hovered (2.5:1).
- `tests/e2e/a11y.spec.ts` now fails on any `color-contrast` violation. After the change: 0 on the same 17 addresses in both themes, and on the five overlays.

Verdicts that say how sure they are, detectors that see through disguises, and one command to set up any client
Honest numbers, a lighter footprint, nothing done silently
Hostile input, honest verdicts, a harder release path
